teile.einleitung: The League of Nations was an organisation of states founded after the First World War to secure peace. It is seen as the forerunner of today's UN and was based in Geneva. However, it could not prevent the Second World War.
wichtigste: The League of Nations was the forerunner of the UN after the First World War.
It was founded in 1920 and was based in Geneva.
The idea came mainly from the American president Woodrow Wilson.
Even so, the USA never joined the League of Nations.
Switzerland became a member in 1920 after a popular vote.
Germany, Japan and Italy left the League of Nations in the 1930s.
The League of Nations was dissolved in 1946 and the UN took over its tasks.

abschnitte.text: The First World War from 1914 to 1918 was the worst war in history up to that time. The US president **Woodrow Wilson** suggested founding a community of states that would prevent future wars. The Covenant of the League of Nations became part of the peace treaties of 1919, such as the Treaty of Versailles. The League of Nations began its work on 10 January 1920.

**Geneva** was chosen as its seat, partly because of Swiss neutrality. At first the League of Nations worked in a former hotel by the lake, which was later called the Palais Wilson. In the 1930s the large **Palais des Nations** was built in Ariana Park. Today this building is the UN's European headquarters.

abschnitte.titel: Switzerland in the League of Nations
abschnitte.text: On 16 May 1920 the people and the cantons approved Switzerland joining. Switzerland was allowed to keep a special form of neutrality: it took part in economic sanctions, but not in military ones. It gave up this **differential neutrality** again in 1938 and returned to full neutrality. Many international experts and diplomats lived in Geneva at that time.

The League of Nations had no troops of its own and depended on the goodwill of the states. The USA never joined, and the Soviet Union was only a member from 1934 to 1939. Germany joined in 1926 and left again in 1933, as did Japan in 1933. When Italy invaded Abyssinia, today's Ethiopia, in 1935, the **sanctions** were too weak. The Second World War showed that the League of Nations had failed.

Despite its failure, the League of Nations also had successes, such as the peaceful settlement of the dispute over the **Åland Islands** between Finland and Sweden in 1921. The Norwegian Fridtjof Nansen introduced the Nansen passport for refugees. The League of Nations was dissolved on 18 April 1946. The UN took over many of its ideas but gave the Security Council more power.

begriffe.erklaerung: The first worldwide union of states to keep the peace.
The basic rules of an organisation.
A state does not take part in other states' wars.
An identity document for stateless refugees, introduced by the League of Nations.

gewusst: Woodrow Wilson received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1919 for his work for the League of Nations, but his own country never joined.
The Soviet Union was the only country to be expelled from the League of Nations, after it attacked Finland in 1939.

t110g3x6.t: Treaty establishing a Constitution for Europe

teile.einleitung: The Treaty establishing a Constitution for Europe was meant to put the EU on a new footing. It was signed in Rome in 2004. In 2005, however, it failed in referendums in France and the Netherlands.
wichtigste: The draft was drawn up by the European Convention under Valéry Giscard d'Estaing.
The treaty was signed in Rome on 29 October 2004.
In February 2005 Spain was the first country to approve it in a referendum.
France and the Netherlands said no in 2005.
After that the EU took a period of reflection.
A “Union Minister for Foreign Affairs” was planned.
Much of its content later went into the Treaty of Lisbon.

abschnitte.text: The draft was worked out by the **European Convention**. It met from **2002 to 2003** and was made up of representatives of governments, parliaments and EU bodies. It was **chaired** by the former French president **Valéry Giscard d'Estaing**. The treaty was meant to combine the existing treaties into a single text. On **29 October 2004** the heads of state and government signed it in **Rome**, in the same place as the founding treaties of 1957.

The treaty named the **flag**, **anthem**, **motto**, currency and **Europe Day** as symbols of the Union. For the top foreign affairs representative the title **“Union Minister for Foreign Affairs”** was planned. Critics felt that such state-like terms made the EU look like a **superstate**.

In **Spain**, on **20 February 2005** around three quarters of voters said **yes**, with a low turnout of about 42 per cent. But then **France** voted **no** on **29 May 2005** with around 55 per cent. On **1 June 2005** the **Netherlands** followed with around 62 per cent no. **Luxembourg** nevertheless approved the treaty on **10 July 2005** with around 57 per cent. Other countries postponed their planned votes.

In **June 2005** the European Council decided on a **period of reflection**, a time for thinking things over. Only in **2007** was agreement reached on a new reform project **without the word constitution**. This became the **Treaty of Lisbon**. Symbols such as the flag and anthem were left out of the new treaty text but are still used in everyday life. The title “Foreign Minister” was also dropped, but the tasks largely remained under a different name.

gewusst: France and the Netherlands, which said no, were both among the six founding states of European integration.
The European anthem is the melody of the “Ode to Joy” from Beethoven's Ninth Symphony.

teile.einleitung: The European Union was founded with the Treaty of Maastricht. It was signed in 1992 in the Dutch city of Maastricht. It also prepared the way for the euro and introduced citizenship of the Union.
wichtigste: The treaty was signed on 7 February 1992.
It came into force on 1 November 1993.
It created the European Union.
It set out the path to economic and monetary union and the euro.
It introduced citizenship of the Union.
Afterwards the EU rested on three pillars.
Denmark said no in a first referendum.

abschnitte.text: **Maastricht** lies in the south of the **Netherlands**, near the borders with Belgium and Germany. The **Treaty on European Union** was signed there on **7 February 1992**. After ratification in all member states it came into force on **1 November 1993**. It is regarded as the **founding treaty** of the EU.

The structure of the EU is often described with a **three-pillar model**. The **first pillar** was the **European Communities**. The **second pillar** was the **Common Foreign and Security Policy** (CFSP). The **third pillar** was cooperation in **justice and home affairs**. The second and third pillars were organised on an **intergovernmental** basis, so the governments kept more power there.

The treaty set out the path to **economic and monetary union**. This gave rise to the **euro**, which has also been used as cash since 2002. Any country that wants to introduce the euro must meet the **Maastricht criteria**. One of them: the annual **government deficit** may be no more than **3 per cent** of gross domestic product. Gross domestic product is the value of all the goods and services of a country in one year.

Maastricht brought **citizenship of the Union**. Every person who holds the nationality of an EU country is at the same time a **citizen of the Union**. This means, for example, that you may move freely in other EU countries and vote in local elections where you live. Citizenship of the Union adds to your own nationality but does not replace it.

In **Denmark** voters narrowly said **no** in the first vote in **1992**. After **special arrangements** for Denmark they approved it in a second vote. In **Switzerland**, too, there was a vote on Europe at that time: on **6 December 1992** the people and the cantons rejected joining the **European Economic Area**.

gewusst: Euro coins and banknotes only arrived in people's purses and wallets around ten years after Maastricht was signed.
Denmark still has an exemption today and has not introduced the euro.

teile.einleitung: In ancient **Athens**, one of the first democracies in the world came into being around 2500 years ago. The citizens voted on laws themselves and filled many offices by drawing lots. However, only a small part of the population was allowed to take part.
wichtigste: Around 594 BC Solon abolished debt slavery.
With his reforms around 508 BC, Cleisthenes is regarded as the founder of democracy.
The people's assembly was called the Ekklesia and usually met on the Pnyx hill.
The council (Boule) had 500 members.
In the people's court, the Heliaia, jurors chosen by lot gave judgment.
Many offices were filled by drawing lots.
Only adult male citizens were allowed to vote.

abschnitte.text: Around 594 BC **Solon** carried out important reforms. He banned Athenians from becoming slaves because of debts, which was called **debt slavery**. Around 508 BC **Cleisthenes** reorganised the citizens into ten **tribes** (phylai). This weakened old power groups. That is why Cleisthenes is regarded as the founder of Athenian democracy. Under **Pericles** it had its golden age in the 5th century BC.

The citizens of Athens gathered in the **Ekklesia**. They decided on laws and on war and peace. They usually met on the **Pnyx**, a hill west of the Acropolis. There was room there for thousands of citizens. Every citizen was allowed to speak and make proposals. Votes were often taken by raising hands.

The **council**, the Boule, had 500 members. Each of the ten tribes provided 50 of them. The council prepared the decisions of the people's assembly. In the people's court, the **Heliaia**, often several hundred citizens chosen by lot gave judgment as jurors. Many offices were filled by **drawing lots**, so that all citizens had the same chance. Only a few offices, such as the ten generals, the **strategoi**, were elected.

abschnitte.titel: Who was not allowed to take part?
abschnitte.text: Only **adult male citizens** were allowed to have a say. Women were excluded, as were **slaves**. The **metics**, foreigners who had moved there, also had no citizenship. They lived and worked in Athens and paid taxes but were not allowed to have a political say. So only a small part of the population took part in the democracy.

A special institution was **ostracism**, in Greek ostrakismos. The citizens scratched the name of a politician onto a piece of broken pottery. Whoever received the most votes had to leave the city for ten years. This was meant to stop anyone from becoming too powerful. Archaeologists have found many such pieces of pottery.

gewusst: The word “democracy” comes from Greek and means “rule by the people”.
To choose the jurors by lot, the Athenians used a stone lottery machine, the kleroterion.

teile.einleitung: Before a vote all voters are sent a **voting envelope** at home. With it you can easily vote by post. But there are a few rules you have to follow.
wichtigste: The municipality sends the voting envelope to people's homes by post.
The envelope contains the ballot paper and the voting card.
If the voting card is not in the envelope, the vote does not count.
Today most people in Switzerland vote by post.
You may send the envelope back as soon as you have filled it in.
The envelope must reach the municipality before voting closes.

abschnitte.text: A few weeks before the vote the **municipality** sends out the voting papers by **post**. Every **voter** receives their own envelope. In Switzerland anyone who is a Swiss citizen and at least 18 years old may vote at federal level. The papers also include explanations of the proposals.

The voting envelope contains the **ballot paper** and the **voting card**. On the ballot paper there is a question for each proposal. You fill it in and write yes or no. The voting card shows that you are allowed to vote. In many cantons you have to sign it.

First you fill in the ballot paper and put it in the small ballot envelope. Then everything goes into the large envelope together with the **voting card**. If the voting card is missing, **the vote does not count**. You may send the envelope back early, as soon as it is filled in. You can put it in a post box or in the **municipality's letter box**.

The envelope must reach the municipality **before voting closes**. If someone sends it too late, their vote no longer counts. That is why you should post it a few days before voting Sunday. Today most people in Switzerland vote **by post**. Only a few still go to the polling station themselves on Sunday.

gewusst: Since 1994 all voters have been allowed to vote by post in national votes without needing a special reason.

teile.einleitung: The Armistice Agreement of Panmunjom ended the fighting in the Korean War in 1953. A peace treaty was never signed afterwards. That is why, legally speaking, North and South Korea are still at war today, and Switzerland has helped to monitor the armistice since 1953.
wichtigste: The armistice ended the fighting of the Korean War.
It was signed on 27 July 1953 in the border village of Panmunjom.
It was signed by the UN Command, North Korea and China, but not by South Korea.
A peace treaty was never concluded.
Since then the Demilitarised Zone has separated North and South Korea.
Since 1953 Switzerland and Sweden have had officers on the supervisory commission.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War Korea was divided into a northern and a southern part. In June **1950** North Korean troops invaded South Korea. This began the **Korean War**. UN troops led by the USA came to South Korea's aid, while China supported North Korea. After three years of war the front line ran roughly where the border had been before.

The armistice was signed in **Panmunjom** on **27 July 1953**. It was signed by the US-led **UN Command**, **North Korea** and **China**. The South Korean president wanted to keep fighting and refused to sign. An **armistice** means that the fighting stops. But a peace treaty that officially ends the war was never concluded.

Since 1953 the **Demilitarised Zone** has separated the two states. It is about 4 kilometres wide and about 250 kilometres long. “Demilitarised” means that actually no soldiers or weapons are allowed there. But there are many troops on both sides. The border is therefore considered one of the most heavily guarded in the world.

To monitor the armistice, the **Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission** was set up. Originally it consisted of Switzerland, Sweden, Poland and Czechoslovakia. To this day, officers from **Switzerland** and **Sweden** are there. The Swiss delegation is the Swiss Army's oldest mission abroad. It shows how Switzerland uses its neutrality for peace.

Panmunjom is still a place for talks between the two Koreas today. In April **2018** the South Korean president **Moon Jae-in** and the North Korean ruler **Kim Jong-un** met there. Kim briefly stepped onto South Korean soil. The meeting raised hopes of peace, but no peace treaty came about.

gewusst: The Swiss officers in Korea have been on duty without a break since 1953.
Because there is only an armistice, the Korean War has, legally speaking, not ended for more than 70 years.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is a multilingual country, and this can also be seen in the state. For its official texts the Confederation uses three official languages: German, French and Italian. Romansh is an official language when the Confederation deals with Romansh-speaking people.
wichtigste: For its official texts the Confederation uses three official languages: German, French and Italian.
Romansh is a partial official language for contact with Romansh speakers.
There are four national languages, named in Article 4 of the Federal Constitution.
The official languages are set out in Article 70 of the Federal Constitution.
Federal laws are equally valid in all three official languages.
Each canton decides on its own official languages.
Bern, Fribourg and Valais are bilingual, and the Grisons is trilingual.

abschnitte.text: An **official language** is the language in which a state writes its laws, sends letters and speaks to people. It is distinguished from the **national languages**, the languages that belong to the country. Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. Of these, German, French and Italian are full official languages for the Confederation.

The Confederation's official languages are set out in **Article 70** of the Federal Constitution. There Romansh is named as an official language in dealings with people who speak Romansh. That is why it is sometimes called a **partial official language**. So anyone who speaks Romansh may write to the Confederation in Romansh.

All laws, voting booklets and many federal websites appear in several languages. Many **translators** work in the federal administration for this. Each language version of a law is equally binding. In parliament everyone may speak in their own language, and there are **simultaneous interpreters**.

The cantons decide for themselves which official languages they have. Most cantons are monolingual, for example Zurich in German, Geneva in French and Ticino in Italian. Bern, Fribourg and Valais are **bilingual**, and with German, Romansh and Italian the Grisons is the only **trilingual** canton. The town of Biel/Bienne is regarded as the largest bilingual town in Switzerland.

About 60 per cent of people in Switzerland mainly speak German, usually as **Swiss German** in everyday life. Around a quarter speak French and about one person in twelve speaks Italian. Fewer than one per cent speak Romansh as their main language. Many other languages are also spoken, for example English, Portuguese or Albanian.

begriffe.erklaerung: The language the state uses for official texts and contacts.
A language that officially belongs to the country.
A language that is an official language only in certain cases.
The line where one language region turns into another.

gewusst: The border between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland is jokingly called the “Röstigraben” (rösti ditch).
In the town of Biel/Bienne the street signs are bilingual.
Romansh has several written varieties; for official texts there is the common form Rumantsch Grischun.

teile.einleitung: The United Nations, UN for short, is the largest organisation of states in the world. Its most important aim is to secure peace all over the world and to encourage cooperation between countries. Almost all the states on Earth are members, including Switzerland.
wichtigste: The UN aims to secure peace all over the world.
It was founded in 1945 after the Second World War.
Today 193 states are members of the UN.
The name “United Nations” means that countries have joined together in order to act together.
Its headquarters are in New York; Geneva is an important location.
The UN has six official languages: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish.
Switzerland has been a member since 2002.

abschnitte.text: The Second World War cost many millions of people their lives. Afterwards the states wanted to prevent anything like it from ever happening again. On 26 June 1945, 50 states signed the **UN Charter** in San Francisco; Poland joined as the 51st founding member. It came into force on 24 October 1945, which is why this day is United Nations Day. The name had been suggested by the American president Franklin D. Roosevelt.

The UN wants to secure **world peace** and settle conflicts peacefully. It works for human rights, which were set down in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. It also helps with hunger, diseases and natural disasters. Since 2015 it has been pursuing the **2030 Agenda** with 17 goals for sustainable development, for example zero hunger and quality education.

The UN has six main bodies. All states are represented in the **General Assembly**, and the **Security Council** is responsible for peace and security. In addition there are the Economic and Social Council, the International Court of Justice in The Hague, the Secretariat and the Trusteeship Council, which is inactive today. The Secretariat is led by the Secretary-General; since 2017 this has been António Guterres from Portugal, whose term ends at the end of 2026.

The UN includes many specialised agencies and programmes. Examples are the World Health Organization (WHO), the children's agency UNICEF, the refugee agency UNHCR and UNESCO. In conflicts the UN sends peacekeeping troops, who are called **Blue Helmets** because of their light blue helmets. The UN flag shows a map of the world surrounded by olive branches as a sign of peace.

For a long time Switzerland stayed outside the UN because of its neutrality. In 1986 the people still clearly rejected joining. On 3 March 2002 they narrowly agreed, and in September 2002 Switzerland became a member. Apart from New York, **Geneva** is the most important UN location, with the Palais des Nations and many organisations. From 2023 to 2024 Switzerland even sat on the Security Council.

begriffe.erklaerung: A founding treaty that sets out the aims and rules of an organisation.
The highest official of the UN, who leads its administration.
A country that has joined an organisation.
A UN plan with 17 goals for a better world by the year 2030.

gewusst: Switzerland was the first country to join the UN through a popular vote.
In front of the Palais des Nations in Geneva stands the “Broken Chair”, a huge chair with a broken leg that remembers the victims of landmines.
In 2001 the UN and its Secretary-General at the time, Kofi Annan, were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

teile.einleitung: The Universal Postal Union makes sure that a letter from Switzerland also arrives in Japan, Brazil or Kenya. It is one of the oldest international organisations in the world and is based in Bern. Almost all the countries on Earth are members.
wichtigste: The Universal Postal Union is known as the UPU for short.
It is based in Bern.
It was founded in Bern in 1874.
Since 1948 it has been a specialised agency of the United Nations.
About 190 countries are members.
It sets rules so that post can be sent across national borders.
World Post Day is celebrated every year on 9 October.

abschnitte.titel: What is the Universal Postal Union?
abschnitte.text: The **Universal Postal Union** is an international organisation in which the postal services of almost all countries work together. It makes sure that letters and parcels are transported across borders according to common rules. Without it, every country would have to make separate agreements with every other country. Its abbreviation is **UPU**.

In the past it was complicated and expensive to send a letter abroad, because every country charged its own fees. So in 1874 representatives of 22 states met in Bern and founded the **General Postal Union**. A few years later it was given the name Universal Postal Union. 9 October, the day it was founded, is now **World Post Day**.

The member countries agree on common rules in a **Universal Postal Convention**. These include each country accepting and delivering post from other countries. The countries charge each other fees for this, which are called **terminal dues**. Every few years the members meet at a Universal Postal Congress to adjust the rules.

The International Bureau of the Universal Postal Union is in Bern. This makes the federal city the seat of a **UN specialised agency**, rather as Geneva is for many other organisations. On the Kleine Schanze in Bern stands the **Universal Postal Union Monument** from 1909. It shows figures passing letters around a globe.

Today people send fewer letters but many more parcels from online shopping. The Universal Postal Union therefore deals with **parcels**, electronic data and the security of items sent. It also supports poorer countries in building up their postal services. Thanks to it, every person has an address to which post from all over the world can be sent.

begriffe.erklaerung: Universal Postal Union, the abbreviation for the organisation.
An independent organisation that works closely with the UN.
A day of remembrance on 9 October, the day the Universal Postal Union was founded.
Money that one country pays another for delivering its post.

gewusst: After the International Telecommunication Union, the Universal Postal Union is one of the oldest international organisations in the world.
Every year the Universal Postal Union organises a letter-writing competition for children and young people.
Member countries must also deliver post from countries they do not get on with politically.

teile.einleitung: On 17 February 2008 Kosovo declared its independence from Serbia. Since then Kosovo, in its own view, has been an independent state. Many countries have recognised it, but Serbia and some other states have not.
wichtigste: Kosovo declared its independence on 17 February 2008.
The capital is Pristina.
Over 90 per cent of the population are Kosovo Albanians.
Serbia does not recognise its independence (as of 2026).
In 2010 the International Court of Justice found no breach of international law.
The Swiss Army has been in Kosovo with Swisscoy since 1999.
In Kosovo people pay with the euro.

abschnitte.text: **Kosovo** lies in the Balkans in south-eastern Europe. The **capital** is **Pristina**, where the parliament and government are based. Over **90 per cent** of the people are **Kosovo Albanians**. **Serbs** live mainly in the north. The **euro** is used as the currency, although Kosovo is not part of the eurozone. Before that, people used the Deutschmark.

For a long time Kosovo belonged to **Serbia** and therefore to Yugoslavia. In the 1990s tensions grew between the Albanian majority and the Serbian government. In **1998 and 1999** the **Kosovo War** took place. From **March to June 1999** **NATO** attacked targets in Serbia with air strikes. After that the Serbian troops withdrew and the **UN** took over the administration of Kosovo.

On **17 February 2008** the parliament in **Pristina** proclaimed **independence**. Many people celebrated in the streets. Many states soon recognised Kosovo, including **Switzerland**. However, **Serbia** still regards Kosovo as its own province (as of 2026). Some other states such as **Spain** or **Russia** do not recognise Kosovo either.

Serbia wanted the question settled legally. Through the **UN General Assembly** it asked for an **advisory opinion** from the **International Court of Justice** in The Hague. In **2010** the court concluded that the declaration of independence itself **did not violate international law**. But whether Kosovo is a state is decided by the other states through their recognition.

**Swisscoy** has been deployed in Kosovo since **1999**. It is a contingent of the **Swiss Army** in the international peacekeeping force **KFOR**. It is the Swiss Army's largest **mission abroad**. Switzerland and Kosovo are also linked by many people: a large community with roots in Kosovo lives in Switzerland.

gewusst: Swisscoy is made up of “Swiss” and “company”, the English word for a military company.
Kosovo is one of the youngest states in Europe.

teile.einleitung: The **Assemblée nationale** is France's National Assembly. Together with the Senate it forms the French parliament. It is the chamber that is elected directly by the people.
wichtigste: The National Assembly has 577 members.
It meets in the Palais Bourbon in Paris on the Seine.
Members are elected in single-member constituencies by majority vote in two rounds.
A regular term lasts five years.
The President of the Republic may dissolve the National Assembly.
The second chamber is the Senate.
In December 2024 the National Assembly brought down the Barnier government.

abschnitte.text: The National Assembly meets in the **Palais Bourbon**, a splendid building on the bank of the Seine in Paris. The Senate sits in the **Palais du Luxembourg**, and the President lives and works in the **Élysée Palace**. Each of the 577 members represents one **constituency**. Some constituencies are in France's overseas territories. French citizens living abroad also have their own members.

France votes using a **majority system in two rounds**. In each constituency, only someone who wins an absolute majority wins in the first round. Otherwise there is a **second round**. To take part in it you need at least 12.5 per cent of registered voters. In the second round a simple, or relative, majority is then enough. Switzerland, by contrast, mostly elects the National Council by **proportional representation**, according to party votes.

As well as the Assemblée nationale there is the **Sénat**. It is not elected directly by the people but by around 160,000 electors, mainly local councillors. Both chambers debate the laws. If they cannot agree, the National Assembly usually has the **last word**. So unlike in Switzerland, the two chambers are not equally strong.

A term normally lasts **five years**. Under Article 12 of the constitution, however, the President can **dissolve** the National Assembly. New elections then follow, and no further dissolution is allowed for a year. Emmanuel Macron did this in June 2024 after the European elections. The other way round, the National Assembly can bring down the government with a **motion of no confidence**, the “motion de censure”.

On 4 December 2024 the National Assembly passed a motion of no confidence against the government of **Michel Barnier**. This had not happened since 1962. At that time it had hit the government of **Georges Pompidou**. Since 2002 the parliamentary elections have usually taken place shortly after the presidential election. This is meant to give the new president a suitable majority.

gewusst: The name “Assemblée nationale” goes back to the French Revolution of 1789, when deputies declared themselves the National Assembly.
The seats in the chamber are arranged in a semicircle, and the political terms “left” and “right” come from the French parliament.

teile.einleitung: The World Economic Forum, WEF for short, is a yearly meeting of political and business leaders in Davos. Every January heads of government, company bosses, researchers and organisations come to the mountain resort in the Grisons. There they discuss the world's big problems.
wichtigste: WEF is the abbreviation for World Economic Forum.
It is a foundation based in Cologny near Geneva.
It was founded in 1971 by the German economics professor Klaus Schwab.
Its best-known meeting is the Annual Meeting in Davos in the canton of the Grisons.
Every January about 3000 guests from all over the world come together there.
Topics such as the economy, climate, health and technology are discussed.
The WEF is well known, but it is also criticised.

abschnitte.text: The **World Economic Forum** is a private foundation that organises meetings between important people from politics, business and society. It was founded in 1971 by **Klaus Schwab**, at that time under the name European Management Forum. It has been called the World Economic Forum since 1987. Its headquarters are in Cologny on Lake Geneva.

The best known is the **Annual Meeting** in Davos, which takes place every January. For several days there are speeches, panel discussions and many talks behind closed doors. The guests include heads of state, bosses of big companies, scientists and representatives of aid organisations. The Federal Council also uses the meeting to receive foreign politicians.

The WEF deals with questions that affect the whole world. These include the **global economy**, climate change, health, poverty and new technologies such as artificial intelligence. Every year the WEF also publishes reports, for example on the biggest risks for the world. However, decisions are not made there as they are at the UN.

Because so many important people come to Davos, a lot of **security** is needed. Police from many cantons and thousands of soldiers of the **Swiss Army** help. The airspace over Davos is restricted during the meeting. The costs of security are shared by the WEF, the Confederation, the canton of the Grisons and the municipality of Davos.

For Davos and Switzerland the WEF is great publicity, because pictures of it go all round the world. Supporters say that it makes talks between opponents easier. **Critics** think that it is mainly the rich and powerful among themselves and that ordinary people have no say. That is why there have repeatedly been **demonstrations** against the WEF in the past.

begriffe.erklaerung: An organisation whose money is used for a particular purpose.
The WEF's big conference, which takes place in Davos every year.
Trade and business between all the countries on Earth.
A conversation between several experts in front of an audience.

gewusst: At just over 1500 metres above sea level, Davos is one of the highest towns in Europe.
During the WEF, hotel rooms in Davos are let at very high prices.
As well as Davos, the WEF also organises meetings in other countries, for example in China.

teile.einleitung: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change is a United Nations body that brings together knowledge about climate change. It does not do research itself but assesses the published studies. Its secretariat is in Geneva.
wichtigste: The panel's English abbreviation is IPCC.
It was founded in 1988 by the WMO and the UN Environment Programme.
Its secretariat is in Geneva.
The IPCC assesses the state of climate research but does not do research itself.
Its major reports are called assessment reports; the first appeared in 1990.
In 2007 it received the Nobel Peace Prize together with Al Gore.
The sixth assessment report was completed in 2023.

abschnitte.text: IPCC stands for “Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change”. In German it is often simply called the **Weltklimarat** (world climate council). It was founded in **1988** by the World Meteorological Organization and the UN Environment Programme. Its **secretariat** is in **Geneva**, at the headquarters of the World Meteorological Organization. Almost all the states in the world are members.

The IPCC does **no research of its own**. Thousands of experts from all over the world voluntarily read the published studies and sum up the state of knowledge. They work in three **working groups**: on the physical basis, on impacts and adaptation, and on ways to slow down climate change. Binding decisions are not made by the IPCC but by the states in their own negotiations.

The major reports are called **assessment reports**. The first appeared in **1990** and was an important basis for the Framework Convention on Climate Change of 1992. Since then reports have followed every five to nine years. The **sixth** assessment report was published in parts from 2021 and was completed in March **2023** with the Synthesis Report. There are also **special reports**, for example in 2018 on warming of 1.5 degrees.

Swiss researchers also work for the IPCC. The Bern climate physicist **Thomas Stocker** was co-chair of Working Group I for the fifth assessment report from 2008 to 2015. This group deals with the physical basis of the climate. Among other things, Stocker studies **ice cores**, which show what the climate was like in the past.

In **2007** the IPCC received the **Nobel Peace Prize** together with the former US vice-president **Al Gore**. They were honoured for their work in informing people about climate change. The Nobel Committee also wanted to show that climate change can endanger peace in the world.

gewusst: The summaries for policymakers are approved sentence by sentence by the governments together with the experts.
The 2018 special report showed that clearly more damage occurs even between 1.5 and 2 degrees of warming.

teile.einleitung: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world. It lies in the middle of Rome and is the seat of the Pope. The Pope is protected by the Swiss Guard.
wichtigste: Vatican City is smaller than half a square kilometre.
The head of state is the Pope, the head of the Catholic Church.
Fewer than 1000 people live here.
The Swiss Guard has protected the Pope since 1506.
The great church is called St Peter's Basilica.
The flag is yellow and white.
Leo XIV has been Pope since May 2025.

abschnitte.text: **Vatican City** lies in the middle of **Rome**, the capital of Italy. It is smaller than **half a square kilometre**. No other country is so small. A wall surrounds large parts of its territory. Vatican City has existed as a separate state since the **Lateran Treaty** of **1929** with Italy.

The head of state is the **Pope**. He is the head of the **Catholic Church** and holds all state power in Vatican City. He is elected by the **cardinals** in the **Sistine Chapel**. In **May 2025** they elected **Robert Prevost**. He took the name **Leo XIV** and is the first Pope from the **USA**.

The **Swiss Guard** protects the Pope. The first Swiss guards came to Rome in **1506**. It is considered the oldest army in the world that still exists. The guards are Catholic **Swiss men** and wear colourful uniforms in **blue, yellow and red**. Every year on **6 May** new guards are sworn in. This day recalls 1527, when many guards lost their lives defending the Pope.

**St Peter's Basilica** is one of the largest churches in the world. The Pope celebrates large **services** there. In front of the church lies the wide **St Peter's Square**, where tens of thousands of people often gather. The **Vatican Museums** with their precious art treasures are also famous. The ceiling of the Sistine Chapel was painted by **Michelangelo**.

Only **a few hundred people** live in Vatican City, fewer than 1000. Many of them are clergy or **Swiss Guards**. No country has fewer inhabitants. The **flag** is **yellow** on the left and **white** on the right. The white part shows two crossed **keys** and the **papal crown**.

gewusst: Vatican City has its own railway station and its own post office, and it issues its own stamps.
Anyone who wants to join the Swiss Guard must have completed recruit school in the Swiss Army.

teile.einleitung: World Water Day takes place every year on 22 March. It reminds us how important clean water is for everyone. Many people in the world still do not have safe access to drinking water.
wichtigste: World Water Day is on 22 March.
It was proposed at the UN conference in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 and first celebrated in 1993.
About 70 per cent of the Earth's surface is covered with water.
Around 97 per cent of the water on Earth is salt water.
In 2024 about one person in four had no safe drinking water.
Because of its lakes, rivers and glaciers, Switzerland is called the “water tower of Europe”.

abschnitte.text: In **1992** a big UN environment conference took place in **Rio de Janeiro** in Brazil. There it was proposed to introduce a day for water. That same year the **UN General Assembly** decided on **World Water Day**. Since **1993** it has been celebrated every year on **22 March**. Each year it has its own theme.

abschnitte.titel: Lots of water, little drinking water
abschnitte.text: Around **71 per cent** of the Earth's surface is covered with water, mostly oceans. That is why the Earth is also called the blue planet. But around **97 per cent** of the water is salty **seawater**. Of the little **fresh water** there is, a large part is frozen in glaciers and in the ice at the poles. Only a small part is available for people to drink.

According to the WHO and UNICEF, in **2024** about **2.1 billion people** had no safe access to drinking water. That is about **one person in four**. Dirty water can spread dangerous diseases. In some areas children have to walk long distances every day to fetch water. And people urgently need water: without drinking, a person usually only survives about **three days**.

Switzerland has many lakes, rivers and glaciers. Large rivers such as the **Rhine** and the **Rhône** rise in the Swiss Alps. Their water flows all the way to the North Sea and the Mediterranean. That is why Switzerland is called the **water tower of Europe**. A large part of Swiss drinking water comes from **groundwater** and springs and is so clean that you can drink it straight from the tap.

gewusst: The River Inn also flows out of Switzerland; via the Danube its water reaches the Black Sea.
Glaciers are important stores of water: in summer they release meltwater into the rivers.

teile.einleitung: The Customs Treaty of 1923 between Switzerland and Liechtenstein links the two countries closely. Since then they have formed a common customs territory. There are no customs checks between them; checks take place at the border with Austria.
wichtigste: The Customs Treaty was signed on 29 March 1923.
It came into force on 1 January 1924.
Before that, from 1852 to 1919, Liechtenstein was linked to Austria by a customs treaty.
The Swiss customs authority also carries out customs tasks in Liechtenstein.
Since 1980 there has also been a currency treaty; Liechtenstein pays with francs.
Liechtenstein joined the EEA in 1995, but Switzerland did not.
Liechtenstein has been part of the Schengen Area since 2011.

abschnitte.text: **Liechtenstein** is a small principality between Switzerland and Austria. From **1852 to 1919** it was linked to **Austria** by a customs treaty. After the First World War Austria's economy was in a bad way, and Liechtenstein ended the treaty. It looked for a new partner and found one in **Switzerland**.

On **29 March 1923** Switzerland and Liechtenstein signed the **Customs Treaty**. It came into force on **1 January 1924**. Since then the two countries have formed a **common customs territory**. Liechtenstein thus became part of the Swiss economic area. That is why many Swiss laws, for example on customs, also apply in Liechtenstein.

abschnitte.titel: Checks at the border with Austria
abschnitte.text: Because the two countries form one customs territory, there are **no customs checks** between Switzerland and Liechtenstein. Checks take place at the **border with Austria**. Switzerland carries out this task. Today the **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security** is responsible for it. Since Liechtenstein joined the **Schengen Area** at the end of **2011**, there have been no systematic checks on people there.

Liechtenstein has used the **Swiss franc** since the 1920s. But a formal **currency treaty** was only concluded in **1980**. In 1995 Liechtenstein joined the **European Economic Area** (EEA), whereas Switzerland did not. The Customs Treaty was adapted so that Liechtenstein can be linked to both Switzerland and the EEA at the same time.

gewusst: The Customs Treaty between Switzerland and Liechtenstein has been in force for over 100 years.
Liechtenstein has no currency of its own but pays with the Swiss franc.

teile.einleitung: An international treaty is a binding agreement between states or international organisations. A treaty between two countries is a written agreement that both keep to. Such treaties govern almost everything, from trade and environmental protection to peace after a war.
wichtigste: An international treaty is a written agreement between states that all parties must keep to.
Treaties between two states are called bilateral, those between many states multilateral.
Such treaties have various names, such as agreement, convention, pact or charter.
A treaty is usually first signed and then ratified.
The rules for treaties are in the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties of 1969.
In Switzerland the people can have a say on important international treaties.
Famous examples are the UN Charter and the Paris climate agreement.

abschnitte.text: An **international treaty**, also called a state treaty, is like a contract between people, except that the partners are states. It says what each state must do or not do. A treaty between only two states is called **bilateral**, one between many states **multilateral**. Many treaties concern quite everyday things, for example air links, post or taxes.

First, diplomats from the states negotiate the content. When everyone agrees, the text is signed. After that each state must approve the treaty according to its own rules; this is called **ratification**. Only when enough states have ratified it does the treaty come into force. For many treaties a state can also make reservations or later withdraw from the treaty.

The most important rules are in the **Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties**, which was concluded in 1969 and came into force in 1980. It contains the principle “pacta sunt servanda”, meaning that treaties must be kept. A state may not use its own laws as an excuse for breaking a treaty. Treaties that violate mandatory rules such as the ban on genocide are invalid.

In Switzerland the **Federal Council** negotiates treaties and the Federal Assembly approves them. For important treaties the people can demand a vote with 50,000 signatures; this is the **treaty referendum**. Joining organisations for collective security or supranational communities always requires a popular vote. Well-known examples are the Bilateral Agreements with the European Union, which came into force step by step from 2002.

One of the oldest known peace treaties was concluded over 3000 years ago between the Egyptian pharaoh Ramesses II and the Hittite Empire. In 1648 the **Peace of Westphalia** ended the Thirty Years' War, and it also recognised the independence of the Swiss Confederacy from the Holy Roman Empire. In 1945 the UN Charter, one of the most important treaties of all, came into being. In 2015 almost all states agreed in the Paris climate agreement to limit global warming.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state officially confirms that it will keep to a treaty.
Between two partners.
Between many partners.
The Swiss people can vote on important international treaties.

gewusst: A copy of the peace treaty between Egypt and the Hittites hangs today in the UN headquarters in New York.
Switzerland is the guardian of many important treaties, for example the Geneva Conventions.

teile.einleitung: The Outer Space Treaty is a kind of basic law for space. It was agreed in 1967 and states that no country may claim space, the Moon or other celestial bodies for itself. Space is meant to belong to all people and to be used peacefully.
wichtigste: The Outer Space Treaty is an international treaty from 1967.
No state may claim space or celestial bodies such as the Moon for itself.
Space is to be explored for the benefit of all countries.
Nuclear weapons may not be placed in orbit around the Earth.
The Moon and other celestial bodies may only be used peacefully.
States are responsible for everything their space activities do in space.
Over 100 countries have accepted the treaty, including Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: What is the Outer Space Treaty?
abschnitte.text: The **Outer Space Treaty** is an agreement between states that sets out the most important rules for space. It was worked out within the **United Nations**. It was signed in January 1967 and came into force that same year. It is regarded as the basis of all **space law**.

In the 1950s and 1960s the USA and the Soviet Union were in a race into space. People feared that one country might conquer the Moon or place weapons in space. So the two **superpowers** and many other states agreed on common rules. Two years after the treaty, in 1969, the first people landed on the **Moon**.

No country may declare space, the Moon or a planet to be its territory. The Americans did plant a flag on the Moon in 1969, but that does not mean it belongs to the USA. No **nuclear weapons** or other weapons of mass destruction may be stationed in space. Astronauts are regarded as **envoys of mankind**, and all countries must help them if they are in trouble.

Each state is responsible for its space activities, including those of private companies from its country. If part of a rocket or satellite falls to Earth and causes damage, the country must be **liable** for it. That is why satellites are entered in a register. That way it is known which country an object in space belongs to.

Today not only states but also private companies send rockets and thousands of **satellites** into space. Some would like to mine raw materials on the Moon or on asteroids in the future. Experts are discussing whether the Outer Space Treaty allows this. The growing amount of **space debris** is also a problem that needs new rules.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the rules and treaties that apply to activities in space.
An object in space, for example a planet, a moon or an asteroid.
The path on which a satellite circles the Earth.
Old satellites and rocket parts that circle the Earth.

gewusst: Under the Outer Space Treaty nobody may own a plot of land on the Moon, even though such certificates are sold on the internet.
The International Space Station ISS is run jointly by several countries, very much in the spirit of the treaty.
The Outer Space Treaty has been in force for over 55 years and has never been fundamentally changed.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. Each canton decides for itself which language is its **official language**. The authorities, courts and schools work in this language.
wichtigste: An official language is the language of the authorities and the laws.
In most cantons German is the official language.
Four cantons have only French as their official language.
Three cantons have exactly two official languages.
The Grisons has three official languages and is called Grischun in Romansh.
Many places have their own names in the different languages.

abschnitte.text: An **official language** is the language in which the authorities work, laws are written and letters are sent to the population. The Confederation has **German, French and Italian** as its official languages. In dealings with people who speak Romansh, **Romansh** is also an official language of the Confederation. The cantons decide on their own official languages.

In most cantons **German** is the official language, for example in Uri, Zurich or Lucerne. **Four cantons** have only French: Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Jura. In Ticino Italian is the official language. **Three cantons** have exactly two official languages, German and French: Bern, Fribourg and Valais. The Grisons even has three: German, Romansh and Italian.

Many cantons and towns have their own name in each language. The city of Geneva is called **Genève** in French and Genf in German. The canton of Neuchâtel is **Neuenburg** in German, Fribourg is **Freiburg** and Vaud is **Waadt**. The Grisons is called **Grischun** in Romansh and Grigioni in Italian. In bilingual places such as Biel/Bienne both names are often on the signs.

gewusst: The town of Biel/Bienne is regarded as the largest bilingual town in Switzerland.
All four national languages appear on Swiss banknotes.

teile.einleitung: The voting booklet is a brochure with explanations of the proposals being voted on. Before a national vote all voters receive it at home together with their voting papers. It helps them to form their own opinion.
wichtigste: The voting booklet is a brochure with explanations of the proposals being voted on.
Its official name is “Explanations of the Federal Council”.
It is published by the Federal Chancellery.
It contains the arguments of supporters and opponents.
In it the Federal Council gives an official voting recommendation.
The booklet is published in the official languages and also in Romansh.
The explanations are also available online, in an app and as a video.

abschnitte.text: Before a vote you receive information about the topics in the **voting booklet**. Its official name is “Explanations of the Federal Council”. It explains in simple language what each proposal is about. It is published by the **Federal Chancellery** in Bern.

For each proposal there is a short summary and a detailed explanation. The **arguments** of the opponents or of the initiative committee are printed, as well as the arguments of the Federal Council and parliament. At the end is the **text being voted on**, the exact wording you are deciding on. Charts and examples often help with understanding.

Before a vote the Federal Council gives an official **voting recommendation** to make its position known. Parliament's recommendation is also in the booklet. But voters do not have to follow it. The law requires the information to be **objective** and complete and the other side to have a fair say too.

abschnitte.titel: How does it get to people's homes?
abschnitte.text: The voting booklet is included in the envelope with the voting papers. These are sent out by the municipalities to all voters a few weeks before voting Sunday. The booklet is available in German, French, Italian and **Romansh**. Anyone who wants can also look at the explanations on the federal government's website, in the **VoteInfo** app or as an explanatory video.

It is best to read the short version first to know what it is about. After that it is worth comparing the arguments of both sides. You can also use **newspapers**, radio and television or discuss it with family and friends. Children can also look at the booklet with their parents and learn a lot about politics this way.

begriffe.erklaerung: The topic or law that is being voted on.
The Federal Council's staff office, which among other things organises votes.
The Federal Council's advice on whether to vote yes or no.
All the papers you need to vote.

gewusst: The voting booklet is usually red, so some people call it the little red booklet.
Millions of copies are printed for each vote.
For cantonal votes, the cantons also send out their own explanations.

teile.einleitung: International law is the law that applies between states. It governs, for example, how countries make treaties, settle disputes and what is forbidden even in war. For Switzerland, with Geneva as the city of the Geneva Conventions, it plays a very special role.
wichtigste: International law governs relations between states and international organisations.
Its most important sources are treaties, customary international law and general principles of law.
The principle “pacta sunt servanda” means that treaties that have been made must be kept.
Article 2 paragraph 4 of the UN Charter forbids the threat or use of force between states.
In 1949 four Geneva Conventions were concluded to protect people in war.
The International Court of Justice is the principal judicial body of the United Nations.
The International Criminal Court is based in The Hague.
Switzerland has been a party to the European Convention on Human Rights since 1974.

abschnitte.text: Within a country there are laws passed by the parliament. But there is no world parliament between states, so **international law** comes about differently. States make treaties with each other, or keep to a shared practice for a long time that they recognise as law. This unwritten law is called **customary international law**. The Dutchman Hugo Grotius, who wrote a famous book about war and peace in 1625, is regarded as the founder of modern international law.

The principle **pacta sunt servanda** (Latin: treaties must be kept) is the basis of all agreements. Article 2 paragraph 4 of the UN Charter forbids states to threaten or use force against other states. Force is only allowed in self-defence or with the permission of the Security Council. Some rules are so important that no treaty may depart from them; they are called **ius cogens**. They include the bans on genocide, slavery and torture.

**International humanitarian law** applies in armed conflicts and protects the wounded, prisoners and civilians. It is based on the four Geneva Conventions of 1949, which were added to by Additional Protocols. The first Geneva Convention of 1864 went back to the Genevan Henry Dunant, the founder of the Red Cross. The Fifth Hague Convention of 1907 governs the rights and duties of neutral states in war on land, which is important for Switzerland.

Two important courts are in The Hague in the Netherlands. The **International Court of Justice** is the principal judicial body of the UN and decides disputes between states. The **International Criminal Court**, on the other hand, convicts individual people for the most serious crimes such as genocide and war crimes. It is based on the Rome Statute of 1998 and has been working since 2002. One problem remains: there is no world police that can always enforce judgments.

The Swiss Federal Constitution requires the Confederation and the cantons to respect international law. Switzerland is the **depositary state** of the Geneva Conventions, which means it keeps the original treaties. Since 1974 it has been part of the European Convention on Human Rights, so people from Switzerland can turn to the court in Strasbourg. With its neutrality and Geneva as the seat of many organisations, Switzerland works hard for international law.

begriffe.erklaerung: Unwritten rules that arise because states have kept to them for a long time and regard them as law.
Mandatory rules of international law from which no treaty may depart.
Latin for “treaties must be kept”.
Rules meant to protect people in war.
A state or organisation that keeps and manages a treaty.

gewusst: The Geneva Conventions of 1949 have been recognised by every state in the world.
The International Court of Justice sits in the Peace Palace in The Hague, which was built with money from the industrialist Andrew Carnegie.

teile.einleitung: Ursula von der Leyen is a German politician. Since December 2019 she has been President of the European Commission, the first woman in this office. Before that she was a federal minister in Germany several times.
wichtigste: Ursula von der Leyen has led the EU Commission since 1 December 2019.
She is German and a member of the CDU.
She was born in Brussels in 1958.
From 2013 to 2019 she was Germany's defence minister.
In July 2024 she was elected for a second term.
In 2019 her Commission presented the European Green Deal.

abschnitte.text: Ursula von der Leyen was born in **Brussels** in **1958**. Her father worked there for the European institutions. Later the family moved to Lower Saxony in Germany. Von der Leyen studied **medicine** and worked as a doctor. She is a member of the **CDU**, the Christian Democratic Union. In the European Parliament the CDU belongs to the **European People's Party**.

In Germany she was first a minister in the federal state of **Lower Saxony**. From **2005** she was part of **Angela Merkel's** federal government. She was **Minister for Family Affairs** and then **Minister of Labour**. From **2013 to 2019** she was **Federal Minister of Defence**, the first woman in this office. After that she moved to Brussels.

The **European Commission** proposes laws and makes sure that EU law is respected. The President is proposed by the **European Council**. After that the **European Parliament** must approve with a majority of its members. Ursula von der Leyen has been in office since **1 December 2019**. In **July 2024** Parliament confirmed her for a further **five years**.

In **December 2019** her Commission presented the **European Green Deal**. With it the EU is to become **climate neutral** by **2050**. Her time in office was also shaped by the coronavirus pandemic and the war in Ukraine. The Commission has **27 members**, because each member state provides one, the President included. In December 2024, together with the Federal Council in **Bern**, she announced the conclusion of negotiations on new agreements between Switzerland and the EU.

gewusst: As well as German, Ursula von der Leyen also speaks fluent French and English.
She was the first woman to head the German Ministry of Defence and also the first to head the EU Commission.

teile.einleitung: Before you vote, you should know what it is about. That is what **voting information** is for: the federal voting booklet, newspapers, programmes and the internet.
wichtigste: The voting booklet explains the proposals and contains their text.
The explanations in the federal voting booklet are written by the Federal Council.
The opinion of the other side or of the committee is also in it.
A voting recommendation from a party is a recommendation to vote yes or no.
The authorities also make the information available on the internet.
Anyone who informs themselves can make a good decision.

abschnitte.text: The **voting booklet** comes with the voting papers. Its official name is the **voting explanations**. In it the **Federal Council** writes what each proposal is about. It also contains the **text of the proposal**, the exact wording that is being voted on. The booklet is available in German, French and Italian, among other languages.

The voting booklet does not only contain the Federal Council's opinion. The **other side** also has its say, for example the **committee** that submitted an initiative or a referendum. This way you can compare the arguments of both sides. If the Federal Council **recommends accepting** a proposal, it advises a yes. If it recommends rejecting it, it advises a no.

You can also find information in **newspapers**, on the radio and in **television programmes**. There are reports and debates there in which supporters and opponents appear. The authorities also make the voting information available on the **internet**. Parties and associations issue **voting recommendations**. Such a recommendation advises whether to vote yes or no.

You should inform yourself before a vote so that you can **make a good decision**. It helps to read several sources and to ask: who is saying this, and why? You do not have to follow a party's recommendation or any other advice. In the end every voter decides for themselves and in secret.

gewusst: The federal voting booklet is sent to millions of households for every vote.
Cantons and municipalities also send out their own explanations when they hold votes on their own proposals.

teile.einleitung: An “Ämtli” is a fixed task that someone takes on regularly. The word is typically Swiss and is very common in families and schools. With Ämtli everyone helps, and nobody has to do everything alone.
wichtigste: An Ämtli is a fixed task that you do regularly.
There are Ämtli in families, at school and in clubs.
If everyone has an Ämtli, one person does not have to do everything alone.
An Ämtli rota shows who has which task.
In many families the Ämtli change every week so that it is fair.
Children can take on simple Ämtli, such as laying the table or watering the plants.

abschnitte.text: An **Ämtli** is a small, fixed task. The word comes from the German “Amt”, meaning a duty or office that someone takes on. In Switzerland you often hear it in the **family** and at **school**. In class, for example, there are the Ämtli of cleaning the blackboard, watering the flowers or handing out the “Znüni”, the mid-morning snack. Whoever has an Ämtli is **responsible** for it.

There is a lot of work in a household: cooking, cleaning, washing, shopping. If everyone has an Ämtli, **everyone helps**. Simple and safe tasks suit a seven-year-old child, for example **laying the table**, **drying up** or **watering the plants**. When drying up, you rub the wet dishes dry with a tea towel. Houseplants need water regularly, so watering is a good Ämtli.

An important Ämtli is **taking out the rubbish**. A lot is sorted in Switzerland. **Used glass** is taken to the **bottle bank**, often sorted by colour: clear, brown and green. **Peelings** such as potato peel go on the **compost** or in the green waste bin, if the municipality has one. Paper, cardboard and PET are also collected separately and recycled.

So that nobody forgets their Ämtli, many families and classes put up an **Ämtli rota**. On it everyone can see who has which task. Some Ämtli are more popular than others. That is why the Ämtli often **change** every week. This way everyone gets a turn, and it is **fair**.

gewusst: The word “Ämtli” is a typically Swiss diminutive; in Germany people would rather say “Aufgabe” (task) or “Dienst” (duty).
Glass can be melted down again and again and made into new bottles.

teile.einleitung: Customary international law is law between states that is not written down in a treaty. It arises because states behave in a certain way for a long time and are convinced that they are legally obliged to do so. Alongside treaties, it is one of the most important sources of international law.
wichtigste: Customary international law needs two elements: general practice and a belief that it is law.
The practice of states is also called state practice, in Latin consuetudo.
The belief that something is law is called opinio iuris.
Art. 38 of the ICJ Statute names custom as a source of law.
A state that firmly objects to a new rule from the start is called a persistent objector.
In 2018 the UN International Law Commission presented conclusions on identifying customary law.

abschnitte.text: For customary international law to arise, two things are needed. First, a **general practice**: many states behave in the same way over a long period. Experts call this **state practice**, or in Latin consuetudo. Second, a **belief that it is law**, the **opinio iuris**: the states act in this way because they believe they are legally obliged to. Without this belief, behaviour is only courtesy, in Latin comitas.

abschnitte.titel: The source in the ICJ Statute
abschnitte.text: The **International Court of Justice** (ICJ) in The Hague decides disputes between states. In **Art. 38** its Statute lists which law it applies: international treaties, customary law and general principles of law. Court decisions and the teachings of experts serve only as aids. Customary law is described there as evidence of a general practice accepted as law.

The **Lotus case** of 1927 was about a collision between a French and a Turkish ship. The court of the time stated that restrictions on the freedom of states cannot simply be presumed. In the **Asylum case** of 1950, Colombia relied on a regional customary law in Latin America against Peru, but could not prove it. In the **North Sea Continental Shelf cases** of 1969, the ICJ required a widespread and consistent practice supported by a belief that it was law.

In principle, customary law binds all states. However, a state that clearly and consistently objects to a new rule while it is still forming is not bound by it. It is called a **persistent objector**. This exception does not apply to **ius cogens**. These are mandatory basic rules, such as the ban on genocide, from which no state may depart.

Because customary law is not written down, it is often difficult to prove. People examine, for example, laws, court judgments, statements by governments and votes at the UN. The UN **International Law Commission** sums up international law and develops it further. In 2018 it presented conclusions on how state practice and opinio iuris can be identified.

gewusst: Many rules about diplomats had long been regarded as customary law before they were written down in the Vienna Convention in 1961.
Customary law also binds states that have not even signed a treaty containing the same rule.

teile.einleitung: Crimes against humanity are extremely serious acts committed as part of a large attack on the civilian population. They are among the worst crimes known to international law. The International Criminal Court and Swiss courts can prosecute them.
wichtigste: The act must be part of a widespread or systematic attack on civilians.
Today they are set out in Article 7 of the Rome Statute.
They can also be committed in peacetime.
The term was first used in 1915 in connection with the massacres of the Armenians.
Unlike genocide, no intent to destroy a group is needed.
Apartheid and enforced disappearance also count.
In Switzerland these crimes never become time-barred.

abschnitte.text: In **1915** **France**, **Britain** and **Russia** warned the Ottoman government about the **massacres of the Armenians**. They spoke of crimes “against humanity” and announced that they would hold those responsible personally to account. The term later found its way into **international law**. After the Second World War it was applied in the **Nuremberg trials**. At that time these crimes only counted in connection with a **war**.

An important pioneer was the international lawyer **Hersch Lauterpacht**. He advised the British prosecution at Nuremberg. Lauterpacht put the protection of the **individual person** at the centre. His approach differed from that of the lawyer **Raphael Lemkin**, who coined the term **genocide** and stressed the protection of **groups**.

Today these crimes are set out in **Article 7** of the **Rome Statute** of the International Criminal Court. An act such as murder, enslavement, deportation or torture becomes a crime against humanity if it is part of a **widespread or systematic attack** against a **civilian population**. The perpetrator must know this. A link with a war is **no longer needed**; the acts can also happen in **peacetime**.

The Statute expressly mentions **apartheid**. This means a regime in which one group systematically oppresses another. The term comes from **South Africa**. **Enforced disappearance** also counts: the state arrests people and keeps their fate or whereabouts secret. This method became known, for example, in **military dictatorships in Latin America**. These crimes differ from genocide in that no intent to **destroy** a protected group is needed.

Switzerland also punishes crimes against humanity in its **Criminal Code** (SCC). Under **Article 101 SCC**, genocide, crimes against humanity and serious war crimes are **not subject to any time limit**. This means they can still be prosecuted even after a very long time. In Switzerland the **Office of the Attorney General** is responsible for such cases.

gewusst: Hersch Lauterpacht and Raphael Lemkin had both studied at the university in Lemberg, today's Lviv.
Crimes against humanity can also be committed by groups that are not a government.

teile.einleitung: In a vote many people decide on a question together by saying yes or no. This can happen in a school class, in a club or in a whole country. In Switzerland voters vote on important questions several times a year.
wichtigste: In a vote you say yes or no to a question.
Usually what the majority wants is what happens.
In class people often vote by raising their hands.
In Switzerland there are normally about four national voting days a year.
Votes in Switzerland take place on Sundays.
Many people vote by post without going to a polling station.
How someone voted is secret.

abschnitte.text: In a **vote** a question is decided, and everyone involved may give their opinion. You say yes or no, or you choose between several options. In an **election**, on the other hand, you choose people, for example for a parliament. So voters either vote on questions or elect people.

Votes are often held at school too, for example about where to go on a trip. Usually this is done by **raising hands**, and the teacher counts the hands. If 14 children want to go to the zoo and 8 children want to go to the museum, the trip goes to the zoo. This way children learn that the **majority** decides, even if they voted differently themselves.

In most votes the side with more votes wins. It is called an **absolute majority** when more than half of the valid votes go to one side. Some questions need more, for example a two-thirds majority. It is important that the losers also accept the result and that the **minority** is still respected.

In Switzerland Swiss citizens aged 18 and over may vote on laws and changes to the constitution. Normally there is a national **voting Sunday** about four times a year. Often there are also votes on questions of the cantons and municipalities on the same day. The cantons of Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden still have the **Landsgemeinde**, where people vote in the open air by raising their hands.

In a vote, how someone voted is secret. This **secret ballot** protects people from being put under pressure. Most people in Switzerland do not go to the polling station but vote **by post**. But anyone who wants to can go to the ballot box in person on Sunday morning.

begriffe.erklaerung: The larger group that voted for something.
Allowed to take part in a vote.
Nobody has to say or show how they voted.
A closed container into which you put your ballot paper.
An open-air assembly at which everyone votes by raising their hands.

gewusst: Switzerland votes more often than almost any other country in the world.
At the Landsgemeinde, voters hold up their voting card to vote.
Animals such as bees also sometimes make decisions together, for example when a swarm is looking for a new nesting place.

teile.einleitung: World Population Day takes place every year on 11 July. On this day the UN draws attention to questions about population growth and its consequences. Today more than eight billion people live on Earth, more than ever before.
wichtigste: World Population Day raises awareness of questions about population growth and its consequences.
It is held every year on 11 July.
It was introduced in 1989 by a body of the UN Development Programme.
Today it is organised mainly by the UN Population Fund, UNFPA.
According to UN estimates, the world population passed the mark of eight billion in November 2022.
Important topics are family planning, the health of mothers and education for girls.
Since 2023 India has been the country with the largest population in the world.

abschnitte.text: According to UN calculations, on 11 July 1987 **five billion people** lived on Earth for the first time. This “Day of Five Billion” attracted great attention around the world. So in 1989 the Governing Council of the UN Development Programme decided to mark 11 July every year as **World Population Day**. Since then the day has had a different theme each year.

For a long time humanity grew only slowly; only around the year 1800 were there about one billion people. Thanks to better medicine, hygiene and farming, the number then rose faster and faster. In 1987 there were five billion, and in November 2022, according to UN estimates, eight billion. The UN expects the **world population** to reach its peak at about 10 billion in the 2080s.

In many African countries women still have many children on average, and the population is growing fast. In Europe, Japan or South Korea, on the other hand, there are few births and people are getting older and older. In 2023 India overtook China as the **country with the largest population**; both have over 1.4 billion inhabitants. Both developments bring challenges, such as having enough schools or enough care for old people.

World Population Day is not just about numbers but about people's rights. Women and couples should be able to decide for themselves whether and when to have children; this is called **family planning**. Good healthcare for mothers and babies and education for girls are also important. There is also discussion about how enough food, water and energy can be provided for everyone without destroying the environment.

About nine million people live in Switzerland (as of 2025). The population grows mainly through **immigration**, because fewer children are born than would be needed for growth on its own. At the same time life expectancy is rising; it is among the highest in the world. The Federal Statistical Office in Neuchâtel records these figures and makes forecasts for the future.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number of people increases because more are born than die or because people move into a country.
People decide for themselves whether and when to have children.
How many years people live on average.
The United Nations Population Fund.

gewusst: According to UN estimates, the eight billionth person was born on 15 November 2022.
It took over 100 years to go from the first to the second billion people, but only about eleven years from the seventh to the eighth billion.

teile.einleitung: The Treaty of Amsterdam is a reform treaty of the European Union. It was signed in 1997 and came into force in 1999. It strengthened the European Parliament and made Schengen part of EU law.
wichtigste: The treaty was signed on 2 October 1997.
It came into force on 1 May 1999.
The Schengen acquis was taken over into EU law.
Javier Solana became the first High Representative for foreign policy.
The European Parliament was strengthened through more co-decision.
A chapter on employment and enhanced cooperation were added.
An area of freedom, security and justice became a goal.

abschnitte.text: The **Treaty of Amsterdam** amended the existing EU treaties, above all the **Treaty of Maastricht**. It was signed on **2 October 1997** and came into force on **1 May 1999**. The aim was to make the EU more democratic and better able to act. In addition, the articles of the treaties were renumbered.

The **Schengen Agreements** on open internal borders had come about outside the EU treaties. Amsterdam took this **Schengen acquis** over into **EU law**. Areas such as **asylum**, **immigration** and **visas** were moved to the Community level. As an overarching goal the treaty named an **area of freedom, security and justice**. Switzerland has applied Schengen since 2008 as an associated country without being an EU member.

The treaty extended the **co-decision procedure** to many areas and simplified it. This put the **European Parliament** on an equal footing with the **Council** on many legislative questions. Amsterdam also created the office of **High Representative** for the Common Foreign and Security Policy. The first holder of the office, from **1999 to 2009**, was the Spaniard **Javier Solana**, previously Secretary General of NATO.

Because of high **unemployment**, a new **chapter on employment** was added to the EC Treaty. The member states committed themselves to coordinating their employment policies. This gave rise to the **European Employment Strategy**. **Enhanced cooperation** was also new: a group of states may go ahead in one area without all of them taking part. Later it was used, for example, for the **EU patent**.

Amsterdam also created a procedure that today is found in **Article 7** of the EU Treaty. If a member state seriously and persistently breaches the **basic values** such as democracy or the rule of law, certain rights can be taken away from it. These include its **voting rights in the Council**. **Expulsion** from the EU, on the other hand, is not provided for.

gewusst: Because Amsterdam renumbered many articles, some provisions have had a completely different number ever since.
Javier Solana was the face of EU foreign policy for around ten years.

teile.einleitung: The Warsaw Pact was a military alliance of the Soviet Union and its allies during the Cold War. It was founded in 1955 as the counterpart to the West's NATO. It dissolved in 1991 with the end of the Cold War.
wichtigste: The Warsaw Pact was a military alliance of the Soviet Union and its allies during the Cold War.
It was founded on 14 May 1955 in Warsaw, the capital of Poland.
Its members were the Soviet Union, Poland, East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and Albania.
The alliance was the counterpart to the Western NATO.
