There they founded the World Bank and the **International Monetary Fund**. At first the World Bank was meant to help rebuild Europe; its first loan went to France in 1947. Later it concentrated on the development of poorer countries.

The World Bank pays, for example, for schools, roads, power lines and projects for clean drinking water. It also helps in the fight against climate change and with health programmes. The **World Bank Group** has several parts, such as an organisation for the poorest countries and one that supports private companies in developing countries. The World Bank also measures how many people live in **extreme poverty**, meaning on very little money per day.

At the World Bank not every country has the same say. Votes depend on how much money a country has paid in, which is why the USA has the most influence. Traditionally the President of the World Bank is an American; since 2023 it has been Ajay Banga. Critics complain that poorer countries have too little say and that some large projects such as dams have harmed the environment.

Switzerland joined the World Bank and the IMF in 1992 after the people had approved it in a **popular vote**. It leads its own voting group with several countries from Central Asia and Eastern Europe. That is why it has its own seat on the Executive Board, the bank's governing body. Switzerland pays money in and works with the World Bank in development cooperation.

begriffe.erklaerung: Money that you borrow and have to pay back later.
People have so little money that it is barely enough for food and the bare essentials.
Countries help each other so that people in poorer countries are better off.
The World Bank's sister organisation, which helps countries that are short of money.

gewusst: Because Switzerland leads a group with countries such as Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, it is often jokingly called “Helvetistan”.
The World Bank's first loan, to France in 1947, was 250 million US dollars, which was a huge amount at the time.

teile.einleitung: Many parliaments in the world are made up of two parts. This is called a **bicameral system**. Each part is called a chamber and has its own members and often its own tasks too.
wichtigste: A parliament with two parts has a bicameral system.
Each part of such a parliament is called a chamber.
Switzerland has two chambers: the National Council and the Council of States.
The British Parliament has an upper house and a lower house.
The US Congress is made up of the Senate and the House of Representatives.
Often one chamber represents the people and the other the member states or regions.

abschnitte.text: A **chamber** is a part of a parliament. If a parliament has only one part, it is called a unicameral system. In a **bicameral system** two chambers debate the laws. Usually a new law must find a majority in both chambers. This means decisions are examined more thoroughly, but they also take more time.

The Swiss parliament is called the **Federal Assembly**. The **National Council** has 200 members, and large cantons have more seats than small ones. The **Council of States** has 46 members; almost every canton has two seats. Both chambers are equally important. A law only applies if the National Council and the Council of States both agree.

The British Parliament is made up of the **House of Commons**, the lower house, and the **House of Lords**, the upper house. The members of the House of Commons are elected by the people. The Lords are not elected; most are appointed and often remain members for life. The chamber of the House of Lords is decorated in red, and the benches are red too. The person who presides sits on the **Woolsack**, a large cushion stuffed with wool.

The parliament of the USA is called **Congress**. The **Senate** is the smaller chamber and is regarded as the upper house. Each state sends exactly two senators, no matter how big it is. The **House of Representatives** has 435 voting members. Here large states send more representatives than small ones.

In federal states such as Switzerland or the USA, the bicameral system creates a **balance**. One chamber represents the population, so the number of inhabitants counts there. The other chamber represents the **member states**, that is the cantons or states. This means the large ones cannot simply decide over the small ones.

gewusst: The Woolsack in the House of Lords is a reminder of how important the wool trade used to be for England.
In Switzerland and the USA a small member state has as many seats in the second chamber as a very large one.

teile.einleitung: The media cannot decide what we think. But they have a great influence on **what** we think about. **Agenda-setting research** studies this idea.
wichtigste: Agenda-setting means that the media influence what people think about.
The research was founded in 1972 by McCombs and Shaw with the Chapel Hill study.
As early as 1963 Bernard Cohen wrote a famous sentence about it.
Gatekeeping describes the selection of which news is published.
Galtung and Ruge's news value theory explains what becomes news.
Priming, intermedia agenda-setting and second-level agenda-setting extend the approach.

abschnitte.text: Here the word **agenda** means the list of topics that are currently seen as important. The approach says: what the media report on often and prominently, people also consider important. In 1963 the American political scientist **Bernard Cohen** wrote, in essence, that the press may not usually succeed in telling people what to think, but it is stunningly successful in telling them **what** to think about.

**Maxwell McCombs** and **Donald Shaw** founded agenda-setting research in 1972. In the town of Chapel Hill in the USA they surveyed undecided voters during the 1968 presidential election campaign. They compared which topics these voters thought were important with the topics in the media. The match was very close.

Not every event becomes news. **Gatekeeping** describes the selection of which news is published, for example by editorial teams. In 1965 Johan **Galtung** and Mari Holmboe **Ruge** developed the **news value theory**. It names **news factors** such as closeness, surprise, importance or well-known people. The more of these apply, the more likely an event is to be reported.

In **priming**, topics that are currently prominent become the standard for judgements, for example when people assess politicians. **Intermedia agenda-setting** describes how media take topics from each other. **Second-level agenda-setting** asks which **characteristics** of a topic are emphasised. So it is not only about whether something is reported, but also how.

In the past it was mainly newspapers, radio and television that set the topics. Today **social media** also play a big role. There, topics can become big very quickly. Research is studying how this changes agenda-setting. For votes in Switzerland it is important to get information from different sources.

gewusst: The Chapel Hill study is one of the most frequently cited studies in communication science.
Johan Galtung from Norway is also regarded as one of the founders of peace research.

teile.einleitung: A visa is permission to enter a foreign country and stay there for a certain time. You do not need a visa for every country. Swiss citizens can travel to many countries without a visa.
wichtigste: The word “visa” comes from Latin and means “seen”.
You usually apply for a visa at the embassy or consulate of the country you are going to.
Some countries only issue a visa on arrival.
With a Schengen visa you may stay for at most 90 days within 180 days.
Switzerland has applied Schengen since 12 December 2008.
For visa-free travel to the USA you need an ESTA authorisation.

abschnitte.text: A **visa** is permission to **enter** another country. It is often a sticker or stamp in your **passport**. The word comes from the Latin verb **“videre”**, which means “to see”. **“Visum”** therefore means **“seen”**. In the past, an authority used this note to confirm that it had **checked** a document.

abschnitte.titel: Where do you get a visa?
abschnitte.text: Visas are issued by the representations of the country you are going to, that is by **embassies** or **consulates**. You usually have to fill in a form and bring documents such as your passport. Today some countries offer **electronic visas**, which you apply for online. Others only issue the visa when you enter, at the airport or at the border. This is called a **visa on arrival**.

The name comes from **Schengen**, a small wine village on the **Moselle** in **Luxembourg**. The first agreement on removing border controls was signed there in **1985**. A **Schengen visa** for short stays is valid for at most **90 days** in a period of **180 days**. Anyone who wants to stay longer needs a different permit. Switzerland voted to join in **2005** and has applied Schengen since **12 December 2008**. Since then it has also issued Schengen visas.

Anyone from Switzerland who wants to travel to the **USA** for a short time usually does not need a visa. Beforehand, however, you have to apply online for an **ESTA** authorisation. It is valid for short trips as a **tourist** or on **business**. Anyone who wants to study or work in the USA, on the other hand, needs a proper visa. Other countries have similar systems for entry without a visa.

gewusst: The village of Schengen lies where the borders of Luxembourg, Germany and France meet.
The 1985 agreement was signed on a boat on the Moselle.

teile.einleitung: The Special Court for Sierra Leone was an international court. It was meant to punish serious crimes from the civil war in the West African country of Sierra Leone. It became known above all for its verdict against the former Liberian president Charles Taylor.
wichtigste: The court was set up through an agreement between the UN and Sierra Leone.
It was a mixed court with local and international judges.
Charles Taylor, formerly President of Liberia, was sentenced to 50 years in prison in 2012.
Taylor is serving his sentence in Great Britain.
The rebel group RUF was responsible for many crimes.
The rebels financed the war mainly with diamonds.

abschnitte.text: Sierra Leone lies in West Africa on the Atlantic. From 1991 to 2002 there was a **civil war** there. A rebel group, the **Revolutionary United Front** (RUF), fought against the government. It was led by **Foday Sankoh** and was responsible for many serious crimes against civilians. Many people died or were seriously injured, and children were used as soldiers.

Sierra Leone is rich in **diamonds**. The rebels controlled diamond fields and sold the stones through neighbouring **Liberia**. With the money they bought weapons. This gave rise to the term **blood diamonds**. Later, countries and companies created a certification system so that such diamonds would no longer be traded.

The Special Court was set up in 2002 through an **agreement between the UN** and Sierra Leone. It was a **mixed court** with local and international judges. It was based in the capital, **Freetown**. It drew on both **international law** and the law of Sierra Leone. The rebel leader Sankoh died before his trial ended.

**Charles Taylor** was President of **Liberia**. He supported the rebels in the neighbouring country with weapons. In 2012 the court sentenced him to **50 years in prison** for aiding and abetting and planning **war crimes** and **crimes against humanity**. He was the first former head of state since the Nuremberg trials to be convicted by an international court. The appeal confirmed the sentence in 2013. Since then he has been held in a British prison, because **Great Britain** had agreed to take him.

gewusst: Charles Taylor was the first former head of state since the Nuremberg trials to be convicted by an international court.
The term “blood diamonds” is closely linked to the war in Sierra Leone.

teile.einleitung: UNRWA is the United Nations agency for Palestine refugees in the Near East. It runs schools and health centres and provides social help. Two Swiss men led the agency for a long time.
wichtigste: UNRWA helps Palestine refugees and their descendants.
The UN General Assembly founded it in December 1949.
It is active in five areas in the Middle East.
It runs hundreds of schools for refugee children.
Its money comes mainly from voluntary contributions by states.
Philippe Lazzarini from Switzerland led it from 2020 to 2026.

abschnitte.text: After the first war between Israel and Arab states in 1948, many Palestinians lost their homes. The **UN General Assembly** therefore founded **UNRWA** in **December 1949**. It began its work in **May 1950**. It cares for **Palestine refugees** and their descendants. Its mandate is **limited in time** and is **extended** by the General Assembly by a few years at a time.

UNRWA works in **five fields of operation**: in **Jordan**, in **Lebanon**, in **Syria**, in the **West Bank** including East Jerusalem and in the **Gaza Strip**. Its **headquarters** are in **Amman** in Jordan and in **Gaza**. Unlike the UN Refugee Agency **UNHCR**, which looks after refugees all over the world, UNRWA is responsible only for Palestine refugees.

UNRWA runs **hundreds of schools** for refugee children. There are also **health centres** and **social help** for poor families. In crises it also hands out food and other emergency aid. Many staff members come from the region themselves. Only a small part of the money comes from the regular UN budget; most of it comes from **voluntary contributions** by states and organisations. Switzerland also supports the agency.

UNRWA is led by a **Commissioner-General**. From **2014 to 2019** this was the Swiss **Pierre Krähenbühl**, previously director of operations at the **ICRC**. From **March 2020 to the end of March 2026** **Philippe Lazzarini** from Neuchâtel led the agency. He too had previously worked for a long time for the ICRC and the UN. UNRWA's work is judged differently in politics, and there are repeated disputes about its funding.

gewusst: UNRWA is the abbreviation of the English name “United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East”.
Measured by the number of staff, UNRWA is one of the largest organisations of the UN.

teile.einleitung: Slobodan Milošević was a Serbian politician. He was in power in the 1990s, when Yugoslavia broke apart and wars broke out. Later he had to answer before an international court in The Hague.
wichtigste: Milošević was first President of Serbia, then President of Yugoslavia.
In 1999 he became the first serving head of state to be indicted by an international court.
The charges covered Kosovo, Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.
In 2001 he was handed over to the Yugoslavia Tribunal in The Hague.
He largely defended himself in court.
He died in custody in 2006, before a verdict was reached.

abschnitte.text: Slobodan Milošević was born in 1941. In the 1980s he rose through the ranks of the Communist Party of Serbia. From **1989 to 1997** he was **President of Serbia**. After that he was President of the **Federal Republic of Yugoslavia** until he was overthrown in **2000**. At that time it consisted only of Serbia and Montenegro.

In the 1990s the multi-ethnic state of **Yugoslavia** broke apart. There were wars in **Croatia**, in **Bosnia and Herzegovina** and later in **Kosovo**. Many people lost their lives or had to flee. Milošević played a central role in these conflicts. Switzerland also took in many refugees from the former Yugoslavia at that time.

In 1993 the UN Security Council had created the **Yugoslavia Tribunal** in The Hague. In **1999** it indicted Milošević for crimes in Kosovo. What was new was that, for the first time, a **serving head of state** was indicted by an international court. Later, charges relating to **Croatia** and **Bosnia and Herzegovina** were added. For Bosnia the charges also included genocide. The three indictments were combined into one trial.

In autumn 2000, after elections and large protests, Milošević lost power. He was then arrested in Belgrade. Serbian Prime Minister **Zoran Đinđić** pushed through his transfer against the wishes of Yugoslav President Koštunica. On 28 June **2001** Milošević was taken to **The Hague**. Đinđić was murdered in Belgrade in 2003.

Milošević rejected the court as **illegitimate**, meaning not lawful. He mostly conducted his defence **himself**. This made the trial much longer. In March **2006** he died of a heart attack in his cell. Because no **verdict** was reached, he is legally **not regarded as convicted**.

gewusst: Milošević was the first serving head of state to be indicted by an international court.
His trial lasted about four years and ended without a verdict.

teile.einleitung: World Refugee Day takes place every year on 20 June. On this day we remember the millions of people who have had to flee their homes because of war, persecution or danger. It is meant to show how much courage it takes to flee and why protection for refugees is so important.
wichtigste: World Refugee Day remembers people who have had to flee war or danger.
It is held worldwide every year on 20 June.
The UN General Assembly decided on the day of remembrance in 2000.
It was first marked in 2001, exactly 50 years after the Geneva Refugee Convention.
It is organised mainly by the UN Refugee Agency UNHCR, which is based in Geneva.
Today well over 100 million people worldwide have fled or been driven from their homes.
In Switzerland, too, there are events, festivals and meetings around 20 June.

abschnitte.text: **World Refugee Day** is an international day of remembrance and action of the United Nations. It is meant to draw attention to people who have had to leave their homes. At the same time it honours their strength and courage. Many organisations use the day to inform people about the situation of refugees and to collect donations.

Before World Refugee Day, many African countries already had an African Refugee Day on 20 June. In December 2000 the **UN General Assembly** decided to introduce this day for the whole world. On 20 June 2001 it was marked worldwide for the first time. The year was chosen deliberately, because the **Geneva Refugee Convention** had been adopted in Geneva in 1951.

According to the Geneva Refugee Convention, a **refugee** is a person who has left their country because they are persecuted there. Reasons can be, for example, their religion, their origin or their political opinion. Many people also flee war and violence. People who have to flee within their own country are called **internally displaced people**. Most refugees find protection in a country next to their homeland.

The **UNHCR** is the United Nations Refugee Agency and has its headquarters in Geneva. It was founded in 1950 and helps refugees with tents, water, food and protection. For World Refugee Day the UNHCR publishes figures every year on how many people have been forced to flee. In the mid-2020s there were about 120 million people, more than ever before.

In Switzerland there are festivals, concerts and information stands in many towns around 20 June. An important organiser is the **Swiss Refugee Council**. Churches often hold a Refugee Sunday. In Switzerland the **State Secretariat for Migration**, SEM for short, is responsible for asylum applications. The day is meant to make meetings between refugees and local people possible.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who has had to leave their home because they are persecuted or in danger there.
Protection that a country gives to a persecuted person.
The UN Refugee Agency, based in Geneva.
An agreement of 1951 that sets out who is a refugee and what rights they have.

gewusst: The UNHCR has received the Nobel Peace Prize twice, in 1954 and 1981.
The most important rule for protecting refugees was agreed in Switzerland, in Geneva.
Almost half of all people who have been forced to flee are children and young people.

teile.einleitung: Tidying up is not always fun, but it helps a lot. In a tidy room you find your things more quickly and trip over less. With a few tricks, tidying up is quite easy.
wichtigste: If you tidy up, you find your things again more quickly.
Dirty clothes belong in the laundry basket.
Crates and boxes give every toy a place.
It is best to tidy up straight after playing.
Waste paper is bundled up and put out for the paper collection.
Old batteries are taken back to the shop.

abschnitte.text: The most important trick when tidying up: everything has a **fixed place**. Small toys go in **crates or boxes**. Books stand on the shelf, and pencils lie in a box. If you know where something belongs, tidying up is quick. A picture on the box shows what goes in it.

If you tidy up straight **after playing**, you never have a huge pile. That saves time and trouble. It also helps to get out only one game at a time. With music or a little race against the clock, tidying up is more fun. And in a tidy room you can concentrate better.

Dirty socks and clothes go in the **laundry basket**. From there they go into the washing machine. Clean clothes are folded or hung up. When you come home, you put your **shoes** in their place by the entrance. That way they are not in anyone's way, and the dirt stays outside.

When tidying up you often find things that need to go. In Switzerland a lot is **collected separately**. Waste paper is bundled up and put out for the **paper collection**, and new paper is made from it. Old **batteries** contain substances that harm the environment. That is why you return them to the collection boxes in shops. PET bottles and glass also have their own collection points.

abschnitte.titel: Passing things on instead of throwing them away
abschnitte.text: Some toys you no longer need because you have grown bigger. If they are still in good condition, they can make **other children** happy. You can give them away, **donate** them or swap them. Clothes that are too small can also be passed on. This way you have more space, and the things go on being used.

gewusst: In Switzerland, shops that sell batteries must take old batteries back free of charge.
New paper, such as newspaper or cardboard, can be made from waste paper several times over.

tec5ncy.t: Additional Protocols to the Geneva Conventions

teile.einleitung: The Additional Protocols add to the four Geneva Conventions, which protect people in war. The first two protocols date from 1977, and a third from 2005. Switzerland plays a special role because it keeps the documents.
wichtigste: Additional Protocol I applies to international armed conflicts, Additional Protocol II to non-international ones.
Additional Protocol III of 2005 introduced the Red Crystal as a protective emblem.
Switzerland is the depositary of the Geneva Conventions and the Additional Protocols.
Switzerland ratified Additional Protocols I and II in 1982.
Under Art. 77 AP I, children under 15 may not be recruited into the armed forces.
Under Art. 56 AP I, dams, dykes and nuclear power stations are specially protected.
Under Art. 36 AP I, new weapons must be reviewed legally.

abschnitte.text: The **Geneva Conventions** of 1949 protect the wounded, prisoners of war and civilians. After many new wars it became clear that further rules were needed. So in **1977** two **Additional Protocols** were drawn up in Geneva. **Additional Protocol I** applies to wars between states. It also treats struggles by peoples against **colonial rule**, foreign occupation and **racist regimes** as international conflicts. This rule was one reason why some states did not ratify the protocol.

**Additional Protocol II** governs **non-international armed conflicts**, mainly civil wars. It extends Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions. It applies when armed groups under responsible command control parts of a territory. In such conflicts, too, civilians, the wounded and prisoners must be protected.

Under **Art. 36 AP I** states must check **new weapons** to see whether their use would be forbidden. Switzerland carries out its own reviews for this. **Art. 56** gives special protection to **dams**, **dykes** and **nuclear power stations**, because an attack could release dangerous forces. They can be marked with three orange circles. Under **Art. 77**, **children under 15** may not be recruited into the armed forces or take part in fighting.

**Additional Protocol III** of **2005** introduced a new protective emblem: the **Red Crystal**. It is a red square standing on one of its corners, on a white background. It has no religious or national meaning. The Red Crystal has equal status with the **Red Cross** and the **Red Crescent**. This means it can be used by countries that do not want to use either of the other two emblems.

**Switzerland** is the **depositary** of the Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocols. This means the **Federal Council** keeps the documents and receives ratifications. Switzerland itself ratified Protocols I and II in **1982**. The **International Humanitarian Fact-Finding Commission** is also based in **Bern**. It was set up in 1991 under **Art. 90 AP I** and can investigate alleged serious violations.

gewusst: A later Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child raised the protection of children in armed conflicts beyond the age limit of 15.
The sign with three orange circles warns that an attack on this installation could release dangerous forces.

teile.einleitung: World cultural heritage means especially valuable places and buildings all over the world that are protected by UNESCO. They include pyramids, temples, old towns and monasteries, but also landscapes shaped by people. They are meant to be preserved for everyone and for future generations.
wichtigste: UNESCO is the United Nations organisation for education, science and culture.
It protects especially valuable places and buildings all over the world as world cultural heritage.
This is based on the World Heritage Convention, which was agreed in 1972.
As well as cultural heritage, there is also natural heritage for unique natural areas.
There are well over 1000 World Heritage Sites worldwide.
Switzerland has about 13 World Heritage Sites (as of 2025), for example the Old City of Bern.
Countries with a site on the list commit themselves to looking after it well.

abschnitte.text: **World cultural heritage** includes buildings, towns and cultural landscapes that are important for all of humanity. They tell us something about the history, art or life of people in earlier times. Well-known examples are the Pyramids of Giza in Egypt, the Great Wall of China and the Acropolis in Athens. Together with **natural heritage**, this is called World Heritage.

**UNESCO** is a specialised agency of the United Nations based in Paris. In 1972 its member states adopted the **World Heritage Convention**. In it the countries promise to protect their most valuable places and to help each other do so. Almost all the states in the world have signed this treaty.

abschnitte.titel: How does a place get on the list?
abschnitte.text: A country proposes a place and submits a detailed dossier. Experts then check whether the place is really **unique** and well preserved. After that the **World Heritage Committee**, which meets once a year, decides. If a place is threatened, for example by war, natural disasters or too much building, it is put on the red list of World Heritage in Danger.

There are about 13 World Heritage Sites in Switzerland (as of 2025). Cultural heritage includes the **Old City of Bern**, the Abbey of St Gall with its famous library and the Benedictine Convent of St John at Müstair. The three castles of Bellinzona, the Lavaux vineyard terraces and the Albula and Bernina lines of the **Rhaetian Railway** are also on the list. Natural heritage includes the Jungfrau-Aletsch area and Monte San Giorgio in Ticino.

The World Heritage title makes a place famous and attracts many tourists. This brings money but can also cause problems such as litter, noise or overcrowded lanes. That is why countries have to draw up a **management plan** that sets out how the site is protected. Anyone visiting a World Heritage Site should be respectful and not damage anything.

begriffe.erklaerung: The UN organisation for education, science and culture.
A treaty of 1972 in which countries promise to protect valuable places.
Especially valuable natural areas, for example glaciers or mountain ranges.
A landscape that has been shaped by people, such as vineyards.

gewusst: The pile dwellings around the Alps, ancient villages on lake shores, are also World Heritage, and many of them are in Switzerland.
The buildings of the architect Le Corbusier, who was born in La Chaux-de-Fonds, are World Heritage shared by several countries.
A place can also lose its World Heritage title if it is not protected well enough.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland the people themselves decide on many important questions, not just the parliament. Several times a year, usually on a Sunday, voters vote on laws and changes to the constitution. This is called direct democracy.
wichtigste: Votes in Switzerland usually take place on a Sunday.
As a rule there are four national voting dates each year.
Swiss citizens aged 18 and over are entitled to vote.
With a popular initiative the people can demand a change to the constitution.
With a referendum the people can vote on a law passed by parliament.
Changes to the constitution need a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.
Since 1971 women have also been allowed to vote at federal level.

abschnitte.text: In a **direct democracy** the people have the last word on many political decisions. Switzerland is famous for this all over the world. As well as national votes, there are also votes in the cantons and municipalities. This way people can have a say, for example, on a new school or a tax law in their municipality.

With a **popular initiative** citizens can demand a change to the Federal Constitution. This needs 100,000 signatures within 18 months. With an **optional referendum** you can demand that the people vote on a new law; this needs 50,000 signatures in 100 days. Changes to the constitution, on the other hand, always go to the people automatically; this is called a **mandatory referendum**.

abschnitte.titel: Majority of the people and of the cantons
abschnitte.text: For laws, a **majority of the people** is enough, meaning a majority of voters in the whole of Switzerland. For changes to the constitution, a **majority of the cantons** is also needed. This means the proposal must also be approved in the majority of cantons. This way small cantons such as Uri have just as much of a say as large cantons such as Zurich.

The Federal Council decides which proposals will be voted on and on which date. A few weeks beforehand all voters receive the documents at home. Most vote **by post**; the others go to the ballot box on Sunday morning. On Sunday afternoon the votes are counted, and the result is usually known by the evening.

At federal level Swiss citizens aged **18** and over may vote. Women only received this right in 1971, after a vote by the men. In the canton of Glarus young people may already have a say at cantonal and municipal level from the age of 16. Swiss citizens living abroad can also vote if they are entered in the **electoral register**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A proposal from the people to change the constitution.
A popular vote on a decision made by parliament.
The majority of cantons in a vote.
The question or law that is being voted on.

gewusst: About half of all national popular votes in the world have taken place in Switzerland.
Usually fewer than half of those entitled to vote actually vote.
The vast majority of popular initiatives are rejected by the people.

teile.einleitung: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations, ASEAN for short, is a union of states in Southeast Asia. It was founded in 1967 and aims to promote peace, cooperation and the economy in the region. Since 2025 it has had eleven members.
wichtigste: ASEAN was founded on 8 August 1967 with the Bangkok Declaration.
The founding members were Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand.
The secretariat is in Jakarta.
East Timor has been the eleventh member since October 2025.
The “ASEAN Way” is based on consensus and non-interference.
Since its Charter of 2008, ASEAN has had its own legal personality.
The RCEP free trade agreement has applied since 2022.

abschnitte.text: On **8 August 1967** the foreign ministers of five states signed the **Bangkok Declaration**. The founding members were **Indonesia**, **Malaysia**, the **Philippines**, **Singapore** and **Thailand**. Later other countries joined, for example **Vietnam** in **1995** and **Cambodia** in 1999. In **October 2025** **East Timor** became the **eleventh member** at the summit in Kuala Lumpur. The **secretariat** was set up in 1976 and is based in **Jakarta**.

The declaration of 1967 was not yet a legally binding treaty. Only the **ASEAN Charter**, which came into force in **December 2008**, turned the association into an intergovernmental organisation with **legal personality**. This means that ASEAN can now conclude treaties itself. Unlike the EU, however, it cannot make laws for its members.

The **“ASEAN Way”** is typical of ASEAN. Traditionally the states decide by **consensus**, meaning unanimously. They also do not interfere in each other's **internal affairs**. Supporters see this as a way of avoiding disputes. Critics see it as a weakness, for example in dealing with **Myanmar**. After the military coup there, ASEAN agreed a **Five-Point Consensus** in **April 2021**, but the military government hardly put it into practice.

The ASEAN states want to make trade between them easier. In addition there is the **RCEP** free trade agreement (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership). It was signed by 15 states in **2020** and came into force on **1 January 2022**. As well as the ASEAN states, it includes **China**, **Japan**, **South Korea**, **Australia** and **New Zealand**. Through **EFTA**, Switzerland has free trade agreements with several ASEAN states, for example with Singapore and Indonesia.

gewusst: Measured by population and economic output, the RCEP is considered the largest free trade area in the world.
Swiss voters voted on the agreement with Indonesia in 2021 and narrowly approved it.

teile.einleitung: The White House in Washington D.C. is the official residence and workplace of the President of the United States. It is one of the most famous buildings in the world. US presidents have lived and worked there for over 200 years.
wichtigste: The White House stands in Washington, the capital of the USA.
The president lives and works there with his family.
John Adams moved in as the first president in 1800.
The president's office is called the Oval Office because it is oval.
In 1814 British soldiers set fire to the building.
The White House has 132 rooms.

abschnitte.text: The White House stands in **Washington D.C.**, the capital of the USA. It is both the **home** and the **workplace** of the president. It was built in the 1790s to plans by the architect James Hoban. In **1800** **John Adams** moved in as the first president. George Washington, the first president, never lived in it himself.

In **1814** the USA was at war with Britain. British soldiers captured Washington and **set fire** to the house. After that it was rebuilt. The house had already been white before. President Theodore Roosevelt made the name “White House” official in 1901.

The White House has **132 rooms**, as well as many bathrooms, staircases and fireplaces. The best-known room is the **Oval Office**, the president's office. It is called that because it has an oval shape. The **Lincoln Bedroom**, a guest room, is also famous. Abraham Lincoln used the room as a study and signed the Emancipation Proclamation there in 1863, announcing the freeing of enslaved people.

The **Easter Egg Roll** has been held at Easter since **1878**. Children roll eggs across the lawn with a spoon. Before **Thanksgiving**, a harvest festival, the president pardons a **turkey** every year. So the bird is not eaten but is allowed to live on. The president's wife is called the **First Lady**. She also has offices in the White House.

gewusst: The address of the White House is 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue.
George Washington chose the building site but never lived in the White House himself.

teile.einleitung: A right of veto is the right to prevent a decision on your own. The best known is the veto of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council. It gives them great power and is therefore often controversial.
wichtigste: “Veto” is Latin for “I forbid”.
The five permanent members of the Security Council have a right of veto.
The Soviet Union cast the first veto in 1946.
An abstention does not count as a veto.
There is no veto on procedural questions.
The voting rule is in Article 27 of the UN Charter.
Since 2022 the General Assembly has dealt with every veto.

abschnitte.text: **“Veto”** comes from the Latin verb **“vetare”**, which means “to forbid”. Literally it means **“I forbid”**. Already in **ancient Rome**, **tribunes of the people** could block decisions in this way. Rights of veto still exist today, for example for the President of the USA over laws passed by Congress. The best known, however, is the veto in the **UN Security Council**.

In **February 1945** **Roosevelt**, **Churchill** and **Stalin** met at **Yalta** in Crimea. There they agreed on the **Yalta formula**: the great powers should have a veto on matters of substance, but not on procedural questions. In the **UN Charter** the rule is in **Article 27**. Matters of substance need **nine votes**, including the agreement of all the **permanent members**. The word “veto” does not actually appear in the Charter itself.

The five permanent members are **China**, **France**, **the United Kingdom**, **Russia** and **the USA**. Only a **no vote** by a permanent member is a veto. According to decades of practice, an **abstention** does not block a decision. On **procedural questions**, such as the agenda, nine votes in favour are enough. There is also a veto on the recommendation for the office of **UN Secretary-General**.

The **Soviet Union** cast the first veto in **February 1946**, on a question about the withdrawal of foreign troops from Syria and Lebanon. Together, the Soviet Union and its legal successor **Russia** have cast around **120 vetoes** (as of 2026). The **USA** follows with over 80. The United Kingdom, China and France are well below that.

In **1950**, during the Korean War, the General Assembly passed the **“Uniting for Peace”** resolution. If the Security Council is blocked by a veto, the General Assembly can meet in an **emergency session** and make recommendations. Since the **veto initiative** of **2022**, which **Liechtenstein** started, the General Assembly meets within ten working days after every veto. The state that cast the veto is expected to explain its reasons there.

gewusst: In 2023 and 2024 Switzerland was a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council and therefore had no right of veto.
Because one veto is enough, a single country can stop a decision that all the other 14 Council members want.

teile.einleitung: The principle of distinction is a basic rule of international humanitarian law, the law that applies in war. It requires the parties to a war always to distinguish between soldiers and civilians. Attacks may only be directed against military targets.
wichtigste: Art. 48 of Additional Protocol I contains the basic rule of distinction.
Attacks may only be directed against military targets.
In case of doubt, a person counts as a civilian.
Indiscriminate attacks are forbidden.
Civilian harm must not be excessive in relation to the military advantage.
In 1996 the ICJ called the principle of distinction a cardinal principle.
Using civilians as shields is forbidden.

abschnitte.text: The idea is old. The **St Petersburg Declaration** of **1868** stated that the only legitimate aim in war is **to weaken the enemy's military forces**. It also banned small explosive projectiles under 400 grams. Later the principle was developed in the **Geneva Conventions** of 1949 and their **Additional Protocols** of 1977. Switzerland is the depositary of these treaties, and the **ICRC** in Geneva works to make sure they are respected.

**Art. 48** of Additional Protocol I (AP I) requires a distinction to be made **at all times** between the **civilian population** and **combatants**. In the same way, civilian objects must be distinguished from **military targets**. According to **Art. 43**, **combatants** are the members of the armed forces of a party to the conflict, except medical and religious personnel. They may take part in fighting and become **prisoners of war** if captured. In 1996 the **International Court of Justice** called the principle a **cardinal principle** of international humanitarian law.

If it is unclear whether someone is a civilian, then under **Art. 50** the person counts as a **civilian** in case of doubt. A building that is normally used for civilian purposes is also not considered a military target in case of doubt. Under **Art. 51(3)** a civilian loses their protection only **for as long as** they take a direct part in hostilities. After that they are protected again.

**Indiscriminate attacks** are forbidden. These are attacks that are not directed at a specific military target or that use weapons which cannot be aimed precisely. Area bombing of whole cities also falls under this. According to the **principle of proportionality**, an attack is also forbidden if the expected civilian harm is **excessive** in relation to the concrete military advantage.

Under **Art. 51(7)** parties to a conflict may not use the presence of civilians to shield military targets from attack. This is called using **human shields**. If one side breaks this rule, the other side is still bound by its **obligations** towards the civilians. This shows that the protection of the civilian population always applies, even if the enemy does not keep to the rules.

gewusst: The Geneva Conventions of 1949 have been ratified by every state in the world.
According to the ICJ's 1996 advisory opinion, weapons that cannot distinguish at all between soldiers and civilians are forbidden.

teile.einleitung: The Spitzenkandidat principle (lead candidate principle) is an idea for the European elections. Before the election, each European party puts one person at its head. Whoever comes from the strongest party is then meant to become President of the European Commission.
wichtigste: The lead candidate of the strongest party is meant to become Commission President.
The European Parliament pushed the principle especially hard in 2014.
In 2014 Jean-Claude Juncker became the first Commission President chosen this way.
In 2019 the EPP's lead candidate Manfred Weber was not elected.
Article 17(7) TEU only requires the election result to be “taken into account”.
In 2024 Ursula von der Leyen was the EPP's lead candidate.

abschnitte.text: The **European Commission** is something like the EU's government. Under the **Spitzenkandidat principle**, the European parties each nominate a **lead candidate** before the **European elections**. Whoever comes from the most successful party family is then meant to become **Commission President**. This is meant to give voters more influence over who leads the Commission.

The President of the Commission is proposed by the **European Council**, meaning the heads of state and government. It decides by qualified majority. **Article 17(7) TEU** requires it to **take into account** the result of the European elections. But the treaty contains no automatic rule for lead candidates. After that, the **European Parliament** **elects** the person by a majority of its members.

It was mainly the **European Parliament** that pushed the principle in 2014. It wanted to strengthen its influence and make the European elections more personal and exciting. The Luxembourger **Jean-Claude Juncker** was the lead candidate of the **EPP**, which became the strongest force. He led the Commission from 2014 to 2019. For the Social Democrats, **Martin Schulz** stood, then President of the European Parliament.

In **2019** the EPP again became the strongest force. But its lead candidate **Manfred Weber** did not find a majority in the European Council. Instead **Ursula von der Leyen**, who had not been a lead candidate, was proposed. This drew criticism. In **2024** von der Leyen herself stood as the EPP's lead candidate. In July 2024 Parliament elected her for a second term.

gewusst: The German word “Spitzenkandidat” is also used in English and French for this principle.
Ursula von der Leyen became Commission President in 2019 without having been a lead candidate beforehand.

teile.einleitung: UNESCO World Heritage includes especially valuable places of humanity and nature. These include old cities, buildings and unique landscapes. Switzerland also has several World Heritage Sites.
wichtigste: UNESCO keeps a list of cultural and natural heritage from all over the world.
The Old City of Bern and the Abbey of St Gall have been World Heritage since 1983.
Jungfrau-Aletsch has been a natural World Heritage Site since 2001.
The Albula and Bernina lines of the Rhaetian Railway have been World Heritage since 2008.
The castles of Bellinzona and Lavaux are also on the list.
Famous examples worldwide are the Pyramids of Giza and the Great Wall of China.

abschnitte.text: **UNESCO** is the UN organisation for education, science and culture. In **1972** the states agreed on a convention to protect the world's **cultural and natural heritage**. Places of outstanding value can be put on the **World Heritage List**. A committee decides on new entries every year. The countries commit themselves to protecting and caring for their World Heritage Sites.

The **Old City of Bern** with its arcades and fountains has been World Heritage since **1983**. In the same year the **Abbey of St Gall** with its famous **Abbey Library** was added. Since **2000** the three **castles of Bellinzona** in Ticino with the town wall have been on the list. The **Lavaux vineyard terraces** on Lake Geneva between Lausanne and Montreux have been World Heritage since **2007**.

The **Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch** area became a natural World Heritage Site in **2001**. It contains the **Aletsch Glacier**, the largest glacier in the Alps. Since **2008** the **Albula and Bernina lines** of the **Rhaetian Railway** in the Grisons have also been World Heritage. The trains run over many **viaducts** and through **spiral tunnels**, in which the line winds upwards in a circle.

There are more than a thousand World Heritage Sites worldwide. The **Pyramids of Giza** in Egypt are over 4000 years old and have been World Heritage since **1979**. The **Great Wall of China** is thousands of kilometres long and has been on the list since **1987**. The **Great Barrier Reef** off Australia is the largest coral reef on Earth and has been a natural World Heritage Site since **1981**.

gewusst: A World Heritage Site can be put on the List of World Heritage in Danger if it is under threat, for example from war or building projects.
The Benedictine Convent of St John at Müstair in the Grisons has also been World Heritage since 1983.

teile.einleitung: World Book Day is celebrated every year on 23 April. UNESCO introduced it in 1995 to encourage the joy of reading. It also remembers famous writers and the rights of authors.
wichtigste: World Book Day is on 23 April.
UNESCO introduced it in 1995.
Its full name is World Book and Copyright Day.
It remembers William Shakespeare and Miguel de Cervantes, who both died in April 1616.
The idea comes from Catalonia, where people give each other books and roses on 23 April.
The day is meant above all to encourage the joy of reading.

abschnitte.text: **World Book Day** has existed since **1995**. It was introduced by **UNESCO**, the UN organisation for education, science and culture. The day is meant to encourage children and adults to **read**. Many schools, libraries and bookshops hold special events on this day, including in Switzerland.

The idea for the day comes from **Catalonia** in Spain. There, 23 April is the day of Saint George, in Catalan **Sant Jordi**. It is the custom to give each other **books** and **roses** on this day. In Barcelona the streets are then full of stalls with books and flowers. From there the idea spread all over the world.

23 April also remembers two famous writers. The English poet **William Shakespeare** died in April 1616. He wrote many well-known plays. The Spaniard **Miguel de Cervantes** also died in April 1616. He wrote the novel **“Don Quixote”** about a knight who fights windmills because he thinks they are giants.

The day's full name is **World Book and Copyright Day**. **Copyright** protects the works of authors. Nobody may simply copy and sell a book without the authors agreeing. This way writers can make a living from their work.

gewusst: Shakespeare and Cervantes both died in April 1616, but because England and Spain used different calendars, not on the same day.
Every year UNESCO names a city World Book Capital.

teile.einleitung: The **Alpine Initiative** was approved by the people on 20 February 1994. It aims to protect the Alps from growing lorry traffic. Goods traffic through the Alps is to be moved onto the railways.
wichtigste: The Alpine Initiative was approved in 1994 and is now in Article 84 of the Federal Constitution.
The canton of Uri approved it most clearly, with around 87.6 per cent.
The canton of Valais rejected it most clearly.
Aargau was the only German-speaking canton to reject it.
The law set a target of 650,000 lorry journeys across the Alps per year.
Since 2001 there has been the distance-related heavy vehicle charge (HVC).

abschnitte.text: At the end of the 1980s there was debate in Europe about allowing **40-tonne lorries**. At that time a lower weight limit applied in Switzerland. Many people in the Alpine valleys feared even more noise and exhaust fumes. This debate led to the launch of the **Alpine Initiative**. It called for goods transit traffic through the Alps to go by **rail** and for the transit roads not to be expanded.

The Federal Council rejected the initiative. Among other things, it pointed to the **Alpine Convention**, an international agreement to protect the Alps. Even so, the people and the cantons approved the initiative on 20 February 1994. It was approved most clearly by the canton of **Uri**, through which the Gotthard route runs, with around 87.6 per cent. **Valais** rejected it most clearly, and **Aargau** was the only German-speaking canton to say no.

The content of the initiative is now in **Article 84** of the Federal Constitution on transit traffic across the Alps. A law later set a **modal shift target**: no more than **650,000** lorry journeys across the Alps per year. This target has not yet been reached, but the number of journeys has fallen considerably.

Since 2001 Switzerland has charged the **distance-related heavy vehicle charge (HVC)**. Lorries pay according to their weight, emissions standard and the kilometres they drive. Part of the money goes towards expanding the railways. With the **NRLA** (New Rail Link through the Alps), new tunnels were built, including the Lötschberg Base Tunnel and the Gotthard Base Tunnel, which opened in 2016. This means more goods trains can travel through the Alps faster.

gewusst: At around 57 kilometres, the Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world.
The Alpine Initiative association still campaigns today for goods traffic to be moved onto the railways.

teile.einleitung: The **AHV** is Switzerland's old-age and survivors' insurance. It pays people a pension in old age and helps families when a parent dies. Almost everyone who works in Switzerland pays into the AHV.
wichtigste: The AHV mainly pays older people a monthly pension.
Children whose parents have died also receive money from the AHV.
The money comes mainly from working people and companies.
Men normally receive the AHV pension at 65 (as of 2026).
The AHV is the first pillar of the pension system.
In 2024 the people decided on 13 AHV pension payments a year.

abschnitte.text: The AHV mainly pays money to **older people**. This money is called a **pension** and is paid out every month. Men normally receive the AHV pension at **65** (as of 2026); for women the retirement age is also being raised step by step to 65. The word **survivors** means that children whose parents have died also receive a pension, the **orphan's pension**. There are also pensions for widows and widowers.

The AHV's money comes mainly from **working people** and **companies**. A contribution is deducted from every salary, and the employer pays the same amount on top. The **Confederation** also gives money, partly from VAT. The AHV works like this: those who work today pay the pensions of the people who are old today.

In 1925 around **65 per cent** of voters said yes to a constitutional article for old-age and survivors' insurance. A first law failed at the ballot box in 1931. Only in 1947 was the AHV law approved, with around **80 per cent** voting yes. Federal Councillor **Walther Stampfli** is regarded as its most important pioneer. The AHV has been paying pensions since 1 January 1948.

The Swiss pension system has **three pillars**. The AHV is the **first pillar** and is meant to cover basic needs. The second pillar is the **pension fund** through the employer. The third pillar is private saving. In 2024 the people decided that in future there will be **13 AHV pension payments** a year.

gewusst: The AHV is regarded as one of the most important social welfare schemes in Switzerland.
Every person in Switzerland has an AHV number that begins with 756.

teile.einleitung: The WHO Pandemic Agreement is an international treaty meant to prepare the world better for future pandemics. The World Health Assembly in Geneva adopted it in May 2025. It came about as a lesson from the COVID-19 pandemic.
wichtigste: The World Health Assembly adopted the agreement in Geneva on 20 May 2025.
It was negotiated by the Intergovernmental Negotiating Body, INB for short.
It is based on Article 19 of the WHO Constitution.
Before that, only the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control of 2003 had come about in this way.
In a pandemic, manufacturers are to make 20 per cent of their current production available to the WHO.
The WHO may not order states to impose lockdowns or compulsory vaccination.
The agreement comes into force after 60 ratifications.

abschnitte.text: A **pandemic** is a disease that spreads across many countries and continents. During the COVID-19 pandemic many countries were short of masks, tests and vaccines. Poor countries often got vaccines much later than rich ones. So the states decided to work out common rules for the next pandemic. The **World Health Organization** (WHO) is based in Geneva.

In December 2021 a special session of the **World Health Assembly** set up a negotiating body. It is called the **Intergovernmental Negotiating Body**, INB for short. The states negotiated for over three years. On **20 May 2025** the 78th World Health Assembly adopted the agreement with no votes against; some states abstained.

The agreement is based on **Article 19** of the WHO Constitution. This article allows the World Health Assembly to adopt international treaties with a two-thirds majority. Before that, only a single treaty had come about in this way: the **Framework Convention on Tobacco Control** of 2003. Such a treaty only becomes binding for a state when it **ratifies** it, meaning it approves it according to its own rules. In Switzerland the parliament decides on this.

In a pandemic, participating manufacturers are to make **20 per cent** of their current production of vaccines, medicines and tests available to the WHO. At least half of this is to be a donation, the rest at affordable prices. An annex on **pathogen access and benefit sharing** (PABS) was still open. It is meant to set out how samples and gene sequences of pathogens are shared and what the countries of origin receive in return.

The agreement states expressly that the WHO cannot dictate anything to states. It may not order **lockdowns**, compulsory vaccination or entry bans. Each country decides on such measures itself. The agreement can only be signed once the annex has been adopted. It comes into force 30 days after the **60th ratification**.

gewusst: The Pandemic Agreement is only the second treaty in the history of the WHO to have come about under Article 19 of its Constitution.
The World Health Assembly, the WHO's highest body, meets in Geneva every year.

teile.einleitung: UNICEF is the United Nations children's agency. It works for the rights and well-being of children all over the world, so that they grow up healthy, go to school and are protected from violence. UNICEF helps in crises and disasters, but also every day in poor countries.
wichtigste: UNICEF works for the rights and well-being of children worldwide.
The children's agency was founded on 11 December 1946.
Its headquarters are in New York.
UNICEF is active in over 190 countries and territories.
Its work is paid for only by voluntary donations from states, companies and private individuals.
In 1965 UNICEF received the Nobel Peace Prize.
Its work is based on the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child of 1989.

abschnitte.text: The name **UNICEF** comes from the original English name “United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund”. The agency was founded after the Second World War to help starving children in Europe. Later it extended its work to children in Africa, Asia and Latin America. UNICEF has been a permanent body of the UN since 1953.

Every year UNICEF buys huge quantities of **vaccines** and brings them even to remote villages. In this way children are protected against diseases such as measles and polio. For severely malnourished children, UNICEF hands out a nourishing peanut paste that can be eaten without cooking. The agency also builds wells and toilets so that children have clean water.

UNICEF helps to build schools, hand out school materials and train teachers. In war zones it sets up emergency schools and safe play areas for children. It campaigns against **child labour**, child marriage and the use of child soldiers. It is especially important that girls are also allowed to learn.

On 20 November 1989 the UN adopted the **Convention on the Rights of the Child**. It includes, for example, the right to education, to health, to play and leisure and to protection from violence. Almost all the states of the world have recognised this convention, Switzerland in 1997. UNICEF makes sure that children's rights are put into practice.

The committee **UNICEF Switzerland and Liechtenstein** is based in Zurich; it collects donations and informs people about children's rights. With its “Child-friendly Municipality” programme it gives awards to municipalities that involve children especially well. Well-known personalities support UNICEF as ambassadors. The actress Audrey Hepburn, who spent the last part of her life in Switzerland, was one of the most famous UNICEF ambassadors.

begriffe.wort: Convention on the Rights of the Child
begriffe.erklaerung: A UN treaty that sets out the rights of all children.
An organisation that supports people in need.
Protection against an infectious disease by means of a vaccine.
The body gets too little food or too few nutrients.

gewusst: UNICEF obtains vaccines for almost half of all the children in the world.
Audrey Hepburn is buried in Tolochenaz on Lake Geneva, where she spent the last years of her life.

teile.einleitung: Can a country live without an army? Switzerland voted on this in November 1989. The **initiative to abolish the army** was rejected, but it caused one of the liveliest debates in Swiss history.
wichtigste: The initiative was called “for a Switzerland without an army and for a comprehensive peace policy”.
It was launched by the Group for a Switzerland without an Army (GSoA) in 1985.
It was submitted with around 111,000 valid signatures.
The vote took place on 26 November 1989.
Around one million people voted yes and almost 1.9 million no.
Only the cantons of Geneva and Jura approved the initiative.
Turnout was 69.2 per cent.

abschnitte.text: The **Group for a Switzerland without an Army**, GSoA for short, wanted to abolish the army completely. Instead, Switzerland was to pursue a **comprehensive peace policy**. The collection of signatures began in March 1985. The initiative was submitted in autumn 1986. The Federal Chancellery counted 111,300 valid signatures; at that time 100,000 were needed.

On **26 November 1989** the people were able to decide directly on the existence of the army for the first time. The topic moved a great many people, and **turnout** was 69.2 per cent. Exactly 1,052,442 voters said yes, around 36 per cent. Almost 1.9 million said no. Only in **Geneva** and **Jura** was there a yes majority; the other cantons rejected it.

Just over two weeks before the vote, on 9 November 1989, the **Berlin Wall** fell. The **Cold War** between East and West was coming to an end. Many people wondered why such a large army was still needed. Others felt that an army was still necessary for the country's security. The debate was held intensely in families, schools and newspapers.

Although the initiative failed, the result was a surprise for many. More than a third voting yes showed that the army was no longer beyond question. In the following years the army was **reformed** and reduced in size several times. In 1992 the people also approved a **civilian service** for those liable for service who cannot do military service for reasons of conscience. In 2001 the people clearly rejected a second initiative to abolish the army.

gewusst: On the same day Switzerland also voted on an initiative on speed limits.
At around 69 per cent, the 1989 turnout is one of the highest since women were given the vote.

teile.einleitung: A UN Climate Change Conference, also called a COP, is a yearly United Nations meeting on climate protection. Almost all the countries in the world send their experts and ministers there to take action together against global warming. The best-known conference took place in Paris in 2015, where the Paris Agreement was adopted.
wichtigste: A COP is a yearly United Nations climate conference.
COP stands for “Conference of the Parties”.
It is based on the Framework Convention on Climate Change, which was agreed in Rio de Janeiro in 1992.
The first climate conference took place in Berlin in 1995.
In 1997 the Kyoto Protocol was agreed in Japan.
In 2015 the states agreed in Paris to keep warming well below 2 degrees.
Switzerland takes part every year with its own delegation.

abschnitte.text: The abbreviation **COP** stands for Conference of the Parties. This means all the states that have signed the UN **Framework Convention on Climate Change**. They meet once a year, usually in November or December, each time in a different country. The conferences are numbered; for example, COP30 was held in Belém in Brazil in 2025.

At the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 the states adopted the Framework Convention on Climate Change. In it they promised to prevent dangerous changes to the climate. The first COP took place in Berlin in 1995. Two years later the **Kyoto Protocol** was agreed in the Japanese city of Kyoto, giving rich countries fixed targets for cutting their greenhouse gases for the first time.

At COP21 in Paris in December 2015 there was a great breakthrough. Almost all the states in the world agreed on the **Paris Agreement**. Global warming is to be limited to well below 2 degrees, if possible to 1.5 degrees compared with the time before industrialisation. Each country must set its own climate targets for this and make them stricter regularly.

Tens of thousands of people often take part in a COP, including government officials, experts, environmental organisations and the media. Decisions are made by **consensus**, meaning only if no country objects. That is why negotiations often last longer than planned, sometimes late into the night. Important topics are cutting greenhouse gases, money for poorer countries and protection from effects such as droughts and floods.

Switzerland sends a delegation every year, led by the **Federal Office for the Environment**. It ratified the Paris Agreement in 2017 and wants to become climate neutral by 2050. Because the glaciers in the Alps are melting fast, climate change is easy to see in Switzerland. In recent years young people from the climate strike movement have also demonstrated in Switzerland for more climate protection.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas such as carbon dioxide that traps heat in the atmosphere and warms the Earth.
The UN treaty of 1992 on which all the climate conferences are based.
The agreement of 2015 to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees.
Emitting only as much greenhouse gas as is removed from the air at the same time.

gewusst: The secretariat of the Framework Convention, which prepares the conferences, is based in Bonn.
At COP28 in Dubai in 2023 it was decided for the first time that the world should move away from fossil fuels.
Some climate conferences lasted more than a day longer than planned because no agreement could be reached.

teile.einleitung: The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations governs how states treat embassies and diplomats. It was concluded in 1961, and almost all the states in the world have joined it. It is meant to make sure that diplomats can do their work without pressure from the host country.
wichtigste: The Convention was concluded on 18 April 1961 and came into force in 1964.
Diplomats enjoy immunity and may not be arrested.
Even so, they must respect the laws of the host country.
The premises of an embassy are inviolable but do not become foreign territory.
The diplomatic bag may not be opened.
A host country can declare a diplomat “persona non grata”.
Ambassadors belong to the highest class.

abschnitte.text: **Diplomats** represent their country in another state. They work in an **embassy** and look after relations between the countries. The **Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations** was concluded on **18 April 1961** and came into force in 1964. Many of its rules had already been regarded as customary law. With Geneva and Bern, Switzerland is host country to a great many diplomats.

Diplomats enjoy **immunity**. This means they are largely exempt from the jurisdiction of the host country. The police may **not arrest** them or keep them in custody. The host state even has to protect them from attack. Even so, under **Article 41** diplomats are obliged to respect the **laws** of the host country. So immunity does not allow them to break the law; it only protects them from prosecution by the host country.

Under **Article 22** the premises of an embassy are **inviolable**. The police and other authorities may only enter them with the ambassador's permission. Contrary to a widespread mistake, however, this does **not make the embassy the territory** of the other country. The **diplomatic bag** with official documents may also, under Article 27, be neither opened nor held back.

Under **Article 34** diplomats are exempt from most of the host country's **taxes**. However, they still pay indirect taxes that are included in the price of goods. The Convention divides the heads of an embassy into **three classes**. The highest includes **ambassadors**; below them come envoys and chargés d'affaires.

A host country can declare a diplomat **persona non grata** at any time and without giving reasons. This is Latin and means “unwelcome person”. The sending state must then recall the diplomat. In this way a country can react if a diplomat behaves badly, without breaking their immunity.

gewusst: The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations is one of the treaties with the most states parties in the world.
An embassy is not part of the foreign state, even though its premises are specially protected.

teile.einleitung: At the Congress of Vienna in 1814 and 1815 the European powers reorganised Europe after Napoleon's fall. It was especially important for Switzerland: it received new cantons, and its permanent neutrality was recognised.
wichtigste: The Congress of Vienna reorganised Europe after the Napoleonic Wars.
In 1815 the great powers recognised Switzerland's permanent neutrality.
The formal document was signed in Paris on 20 November 1815.
Valais, Neuchâtel and Geneva became new cantons, creating the union of 22 cantons.
Bern received the territory of the former Prince-Bishopric of Basel.
The Grisons did not get the Valtellina back.
The Genevan Charles Pictet de Rochemont worked for a neutral Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The French emperor **Napoleon** had conquered large parts of Europe. After his defeat the rulers and diplomats of Europe met in **Vienna** in **1814 and 1815**. Together they redrew the map of Europe. The leading powers were Austria, Russia, Prussia and Britain, and later France too. The aim was a **balance of power**, so that no state could ever again dominate the whole of Europe.

The preparations were made at the Congress of Vienna. On **20 November 1815** the document in which the great powers recognised Switzerland's **perpetual neutrality** was signed in **Paris**. They also guaranteed the **inviolability** and independence of its territory. In return Switzerland committed itself to remaining neutral in future conflicts. This recognition still applies today.

A neutral Switzerland was in the interest of the great powers. Austria, France and Prussia each wanted to draw Switzerland into their sphere of influence. A **neutral Switzerland** prevented any single power from controlling the important **Alpine passes**. It served as a **buffer** between France and Austria. The neutrality was also extended to **northern Savoy** so that Geneva was better protected.

In 1815 **Valais**, **Neuchâtel** and **Geneva** joined the Confederacy as new cantons. Together with the 19 existing cantons, this created the **union of 22 cantons**. **Bern** received the territory of the former **Prince-Bishopric of Basel**, today's Jura and the Laufen valley. This was compensation for Vaud and Aargau, which Bern had lost. The Grisons, on the other hand, did not get the **Valtellina** back; it went to Austria and is now part of Italy.

The Genevan **Charles Pictet de Rochemont** represented Geneva and Switzerland in Vienna and in Paris. He worked especially hard for a neutral Switzerland. He also helped to write the text of the document recognising its neutrality. Today he is regarded as one of the most important Swiss diplomats of his time.

gewusst: Because there were also many balls and parties at the Congress of Vienna, the saying “The Congress dances” came about.
Geneva has only been a full canton of the Confederacy since 1815.

teile.einleitung: The **two-state solution** is an idea for how the conflict between Israel and the Palestinians could be resolved. An independent State of Palestine is to be created alongside the State of Israel. The details have been argued over for decades.
wichtigste: The two-state solution plans a State of Palestine alongside Israel.
Even the UN Partition Plan of 1947, Resolution 181, planned two states.
The Green Line of 1949 is usually seen as the basis for the border.
Resolution 242 of 1967 stands for the principle of “land for peace”.
The Middle East Quartet presented the “Roadmap” in 2003.
Palestine has been an observer state at the UN since 2012.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, Britain administered the **Mandate of Palestine**. On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly adopted **Resolution 181**. It planned a Jewish and an Arab state. Jerusalem was to be placed under international administration. The plan was never carried out in this form; in 1948 the State of Israel was founded and war broke out.

The armistice agreements of 1949 created the **Green Line**. It applied until the **Six-Day War** of 1967, in which Israel occupied, among other areas, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip. That is why people often speak of the “1967 borders”. Many proposals see this line as the basis, with a possible **exchange of territory**.

After the Six-Day War the UN Security Council adopted **Resolution 242**. It called for Israel to withdraw from occupied territories and at the same time for all states in the region to be recognised. This gave rise to the formula **“land for peace”**. The **Arab Peace Initiative** of 2002, proposed by Saudi Arabia, also builds on it. It offered Israel normal relations if it withdrew to the 1967 lines.

In the **Oslo Accords** of the 1990s, Israel and the PLO recognised each other as negotiating partners. In 2002 the **Middle East Quartet** was formed from the USA, the EU, Russia and the UN. In 2003 it presented the **Roadmap**, a step-by-step plan leading to a Palestinian state. Also in 2003 the **Geneva Initiative** was presented in Geneva, a draft by experts from both sides that Switzerland supported. None of these plans was carried out.

On 29 November 2012 the UN General Assembly upgraded Palestine to an **observer state**. Full membership would need a recommendation from the Security Council, where the USA has a **right of veto**. Many states recognise Palestine as a state. On 28 May 2024 Spain, Ireland and Norway did so together and named the two-state solution as their aim. Other states, including Switzerland, wanted to take this step only later or only as part of a peace settlement.

gewusst: Sweden recognised the State of Palestine as early as 2014.
The name “Green Line” comes from the colour in which the line was drawn on the maps used in the armistice negotiations.

teile.einleitung: Universal jurisdiction is a rule in criminal law. It allows any state to prosecute the most serious crimes, such as genocide, war crimes or torture, no matter where they were committed. Switzerland has also already handed down judgments on this basis.
wichtigste: Under universal jurisdiction any state may prosecute serious crimes under international law.
The place of the crime and the nationality of perpetrators and victims do not matter.
In 1998 Augusto Pinochet was arrested in London on a Spanish arrest warrant.
In 2021 the Federal Criminal Court in Bellinzona convicted Alieu Kosiah of war crimes.
In 2024 it convicted Ousman Sonko, the former interior minister of the Gambia.
In Switzerland the perpetrator must be in the country for this.

abschnitte.text: Normally a state prosecutes crimes that happen on its territory. This is called the **territoriality principle**. Under the **personality principle** it can also prosecute crimes committed by or against its own citizens. **Universal jurisdiction** goes further: for **crimes under international law**, any state may act. These include genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and torture. Such acts concern all of humanity.

In **1961** Adolf Eichmann, one of the main organisers of the persecution of the Jews under Nazism, was put on trial in **Jerusalem**. Israel also relied on universal jurisdiction. In **1998** the former Chilean dictator **Augusto Pinochet** was arrested in London. The arrest warrant had been issued by an investigating judge from **Spain**. However, Pinochet was allowed to return to Chile for health reasons.

In 2016 the Extraordinary African Chambers in **Dakar** in **Senegal** sentenced the former president of Chad, **Hissène Habré**, to life imprisonment. For the first time a court of one state judged the former head of state of another state. In 2022 the Higher Regional Court in **Koblenz** in Germany sentenced a former Syrian intelligence officer to life imprisonment for crimes against humanity.

Switzerland has also held such trials before the **Federal Criminal Court** in **Bellinzona**. In 2021 the former Liberian rebel commander **Alieu Kosiah** was sentenced to 20 years in prison for war crimes. It was the first trial for war crimes before a civilian federal court in Switzerland. In 2024 the court sentenced **Ousman Sonko**, the former interior minister of the Gambia, to 20 years at first instance.

In the **Swiss Criminal Code**, Article 264m sets out when crimes under international law with no link to Switzerland are prosecuted. The person must be **in Switzerland**. In addition, they must not be able to be extradited to another state or to an international court. The **Office of the Attorney General** is responsible for the investigations.

gewusst: The Koblenz judgment was the first judgment in the world on state torture in Syria.
Ousman Sonko is one of the highest-ranking officials to have stood trial in Europe under universal jurisdiction.

teile.einleitung: The World Meteorological Organization, WMO for short, is the UN organisation for weather, climate and water. It makes sure that countries share their weather data. It is based in Geneva.
wichtigste: The WMO was founded in 1950 and is based in Geneva.
Its predecessor was the International Meteorological Organization of 1873.
Countries share weather data through the WMO because the weather knows no borders.
The WMO decides the names of tropical cyclones.
It keeps a list of weather records.
23 March is World Meteorological Day.
In 1988 it founded the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change together with the UN Environment Programme.

abschnitte.text: Clouds, rain and storms move across national borders. Good **weather forecasts** therefore need measurements from all over the world. Thousands of **weather stations** measure temperature, rain, wind and air pressure. Countries share this data through the **WMO**. In Switzerland this is done by **MeteoSwiss**, the federal weather service.

As early as **1873** weather experts founded the **International Meteorological Organization** (IMO). The WMO grew out of it in **1950**. Its founding convention came into force on **23 March 1950**. That is why this day is **World Meteorological Day** every year. Shortly afterwards the WMO became a specialised agency of the UN. It is based in **Geneva**.

The WMO keeps **lists of names** for hurricanes and other tropical cyclones. That way everyone knows which storm is meant, even when several are active at the same time. The lists are used again after a few years. If a storm causes very great damage, its name is removed and replaced by a new one.

The WMO collects the world's **weather records**, for example the hottest, coldest and wettest measurements. Experts check carefully whether a new record is correct. The WMO also observes the **climate**. In 1988, together with the UN Environment Programme, it founded the **Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change** (IPCC). Since January 2024 the Argentinian **Celeste Saulo** has led the WMO, the first woman at its head.

gewusst: The highest air temperature recognised by the WMO was measured in Death Valley in the USA in 1913: 56.7 degrees.
The name of an especially destructive cyclone is never used again.
