teile.einleitung: In every parliament it is laid down exactly who sits where. This seating arrangement says a lot about how a parliament works. Some parliaments sit in a semicircle, others sit directly facing each other.
wichtigste: In the National Council chamber in Bern, the seats are arranged in a semicircle.
A chamber with seats in a semicircle is called a “hémicycle” in French.
In the British House of Commons, the government and the opposition sit facing each other.
The terms “left” and “right” for parties come from France.
In the Bundestag, left and right are seen from the point of view of the presiding officers.
In the European Parliament, members sit by political group.

abschnitte.text: Many parliaments sit in a **semicircle**. This way everyone faces forward towards the middle and can see and hear well whoever is speaking. In French such a chamber is called a **hémicycle**, which means semicircle. This is the name, for example, for the plenary chambers in Paris and Strasbourg. In the **National Council chamber** in Bern, too, the seats of the 200 members are arranged in a semicircle. The president sits at the front.

In the British **House of Commons** it is different. The benches are in two blocks, and the **government** and **opposition** sit **directly facing each other**. Seen from the **Speaker's** chair, the government sits on the **right** and the opposition on the left. The Speaker chairs the sittings. This arrangement suits a system in which two large parties compete against each other.

The terms **left** and **right** for parties come from **France**. In the French National Assembly of **1789**, the groups sat on the left or right side according to their opinions. Since then people have spoken of left-wing and right-wing parties. In the German **Bundestag**, left and right are seen from the point of view of the **presiding officers**. For the spectators it is therefore the other way round.

abschnitte.titel: By group instead of by country
abschnitte.text: In the **European Parliament**, the members from one country do not all sit together. They sit with their **political group**, meaning with members from other countries who have similar views. In the National Council, too, members basically sit together by **parliamentary group**. A parliamentary group is a group of members who work together politically.

gewusst: Because the seating arrangement of 1789 became so well known, we still speak of left-wing and right-wing parties today.
For spectators in the Bundestag's public gallery, the “left-wing” parties sit on the right-hand side.

teile.einleitung: The Genocide Convention is an international treaty that defines genocide as a crime and forbids it. The UN adopted it in December 1948, only a few years after the Holocaust. With it, states commit themselves to preventing and punishing genocide.
wichtigste: In the UN Genocide Convention of 1948, genocide is defined and outlawed as an international crime.
Its full name is the “Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide”.
The General Assembly adopted it on 9 December 1948, and it came into force in 1951.
The term “genocide” was coined by the lawyer Raphael Lemkin.
Genocide means intending to destroy a group in whole or in part.
More than 150 states have joined the Convention, Switzerland in 2000.
Today genocide is also prosecuted by the International Criminal Court.

abschnitte.text: The **Genocide Convention** was one of the UN's first human rights treaties. It was adopted on 9 December 1948, one day before the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It came into force on 12 January 1951. In it the states commit themselves to preventing genocide and bringing the perpetrators to court, whether they are rulers, officials or private individuals.

abschnitte.titel: Raphael Lemkin and the word genocide
abschnitte.text: The Polish Jewish lawyer **Raphael Lemkin** invented the word **genocide** in 1944. It is made up of the Greek “genos” (people, descent) and the Latin “caedere” (to kill). Lemkin had himself lost many relatives in the Holocaust. For years he worked tirelessly for the UN to agree a treaty against this crime.

Genocide occurs when someone intends to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group in whole or in part. This includes killing members of the group and causing serious physical or mental harm. Creating living conditions meant to destroy the group, preventing births or forcibly taking children away also count. What matters is the **intent** to destroy the group as such.

The **Holocaust**, in which the Nazis murdered around six million Jews, was the reason for the Convention. In 1994 hundreds of thousands of people, mainly Tutsi, were killed in Rwanda within a few months. In 1995 troops in Srebrenica in Bosnia murdered around 8000 Muslim men and boys. International courts have classified both acts as genocide.

Switzerland joined the Genocide Convention in 2000. Since then genocide has also been expressly listed as a crime in the **Swiss Criminal Code**. Under certain conditions Swiss courts can prosecute perpetrators even if the act was committed abroad. Since 2015 the UN has remembered the victims of genocide every year on 9 December.

begriffe.erklaerung: The deliberate destruction of a people or group; in German also called “Völkermord”.
A treaty between many states.
The murder of the Jews of Europe by the Nazis.
A court in The Hague that punishes individuals for the most serious crimes.

gewusst: The first conviction for genocide by an international court only came in 1998, against a mayor from Rwanda.
Raphael Lemkin was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize several times but never received it.

teile.einleitung: The WWF is one of the largest nature conservation organisations in the world. It was founded in Switzerland in 1961 and has its international headquarters in Gland on Lake Geneva. Its emblem is a black and white panda.
wichtigste: The WWF works to protect nature.
It was founded in Morges on Lake Geneva in 1961.
Its international headquarters are in Gland in the canton of Vaud.
Its logo shows a panda.
The model for the logo was the giant panda Chi Chi from London Zoo.
In the “Earth Hour” campaign, people switch off the lights for an hour.

abschnitte.text: The WWF is a **nature conservation organisation**. It protects endangered animals and plants, forests, rivers and seas. To do this it supports protected areas, carries out research with experts and talks to governments and companies. It also works for climate protection. The WWF is represented in many countries by its own organisations, including in Switzerland.

The WWF was founded in **Morges** on Lake Geneva in **1961**. Later its international headquarters moved to nearby **Gland** in the canton of Vaud. Originally the organisation was called the “World Wildlife Fund”. Today in most countries it is called the “World Wide Fund for Nature”. The abbreviation WWF has stayed the same.

The logo shows a black and white **panda**. The model was the giant panda **Chi Chi**, who lived in London Zoo at the time and was very popular. The panda was chosen because it is easy to recognise and because a black and white picture was cheap to print. Today it stands for endangered animals all over the world.

In the wild the **giant panda** lives only in the mountain forests of **China**. It eats almost nothing but **bamboo** and needs many kilograms of it every day. Because its forests were cut down, it was seriously endangered. Thanks to protected areas, the number of wild pandas has recovered somewhat. It is regarded as a symbol that nature conservation can succeed.

One well-known WWF campaign is **Earth Hour**. Once a year people all over the world switch off the lights for an hour. Famous buildings also stay dark then. The campaign is meant to show that many people care about the environment and the climate. It took place for the first time in Sydney in Australia in 2007.

gewusst: The panda logo was drawn by Peter Scott, a naturalist and co-founder of the WWF.
Although the giant panda belongs to the carnivores, its food consists almost entirely of bamboo.

teile.einleitung: In the Federal Palace in Bern the members of parliament vote using **buttons** at their seats. An electronic system counts the votes immediately and shows the result.
wichtigste: Each member has three buttons: yes, no and abstention.
Anyone who presses “abstention” votes neither yes nor no.
The National Council has voted electronically since 1994.
The Council of States has voted electronically since 2014; before that mostly by raising hands.
The result appears on screens in the chamber.
How each person voted is published.

abschnitte.text: At every seat in the chamber there are three buttons: **yes**, **no** and **abstention**. Anyone who presses abstention votes neither yes nor no. Only the **member** whose seat it is may press the button. Voting for someone else is forbidden. The electronic system then counts the **votes**.

abschnitte.titel: National Council and Council of States
abschnitte.text: The **National Council** with its 200 members has voted electronically since **1994**. The smaller **Council of States** only introduced the system in **2014**. Before that it mostly voted by **raising hands**, and the votes were counted by hand. With close results this was sometimes difficult.

After the vote the result appears on **screens** in the chamber. You can see how many yes votes, no votes and abstentions there were. If there is a tie, the president of the council decides with a casting vote. This way a vote takes only a few seconds.

You can **look up** how a member of the National Council voted. The votes are published with names. This way voters can check whether their representatives vote as they promised. This is called **transparency**.

gewusst: Before the electronic system, tellers in the Council of States had to count the raised hands.
You can look up the National Council's voting results with names on the internet.

teile.einleitung: The crime of aggression means planning or waging a war of aggression that clearly violates the UN Charter. It is one of the most serious crimes under international law. Only the leaders of a state can be held responsible.
wichtigste: The crime is defined in Art. 8 bis of the Rome Statute.
Art. 8 bis was added in 2010 at the conference in Kampala.
Since 17 July 2018 the International Criminal Court has been able to prosecute it.
Only someone who actually directs the leadership of a state can be a perpetrator.
Only a manifest violation of the UN Charter counts.
At Nuremberg it was called a “crime against peace”.
In 2012 Liechtenstein was the first state to ratify the amendments.

abschnitte.text: After the **Second World War**, leading figures of Nazi Germany were put on trial in **Nuremberg**. There, planning and waging a war of aggression was charged as a **crime against peace**. The judgment called the war of aggression the **“supreme international crime”**, because it contains within itself all the other evils. After that, however, it took decades for states to agree on an exact definition.

The **International Criminal Court** (ICC) in The Hague is based on the **Rome Statute**. At the **Review Conference** in **Kampala**, Uganda, in **2010**, **Art. 8 bis** was added. It defines the crime of aggression. For comparison: **Art. 6** concerns genocide and **Art. 7** crimes against humanity. At the end of 2017 the states parties decided to activate the court's jurisdiction. It has applied since **17 July 2018**.

Aggression is a **leadership crime**. Only someone who effectively controls the **political or military action** of a state can be a perpetrator. Ordinary soldiers therefore cannot be charged with aggression. In addition, not every border incident is enough. By its **character, gravity and scale**, the act of aggression must be a **manifest violation** of the UN Charter.

**Liechtenstein** strongly shaped the negotiations. Its UN ambassador **Christian Wenaweser** chaired the Assembly of States Parties. In **2012** Liechtenstein was the first state to ratify the **Kampala amendments**. The ICC cannot prosecute aggression by citizens of states that are not parties. That is why Ukraine and the **Council of Europe** agreed in Strasbourg in **June 2025** on a **special tribunal** for the aggression against Ukraine. It was signed by President Zelensky and Secretary General **Alain Berset**, a former Swiss federal councillor.

gewusst: As early as 1974 the UN General Assembly described in a resolution what counts as an act of aggression.
The court in Nuremberg was the first to convict individuals for a war of aggression.

teile.einleitung: World Children's Day is a day on which we remember children's rights. It shows that all children in the world have a right to protection, education, health and a say. In Switzerland and at the UN it is celebrated on 20 November; in other countries on a different date.
wichtigste: World Children's Day reminds us of children's rights.
In 1954 the UN recommended that all countries introduce a World Children's Day.
At the UN and in Switzerland, 20 November is the day of children's rights.
On 20 November 1989 the UN adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child.
Many countries celebrate Children's Day on 1 June instead, Germany on 20 September.
Switzerland adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1997.
On this day the UN children's agency UNICEF draws special attention to the situation of children.

abschnitte.text: **World Children's Day** is a day of remembrance and action for children all over the world. It reminds us that children have their own rights and need special protection. Many schools, municipalities and organisations hold festivals, games and events on this day. At the same time, attention is drawn to problems such as child labour, poverty or war.

In 1954 the **UN General Assembly** recommended that a children's day be celebrated in all countries. On 20 November 1959 it adopted the Declaration of the Rights of the Child. Exactly 30 years later, on 20 November 1989, the binding **Convention on the Rights of the Child** followed. That is why 20 November is now the international day of children's rights.

Not all countries celebrate Children's Day on the same day. In Switzerland and at the UN the focus is on 20 November. In many countries of Eastern Europe and Asia, 1 June is International Children's Day. In Germany World Children's Day is celebrated on 20 September, and in Japan there is a separate Children's Day on 5 May.

The Convention on the Rights of the Child has 54 articles and applies to everyone under 18. It includes the right to **education**, to health, to play and leisure and to protection from violence. Children also have the right to give their opinion on matters that concern them. Almost all the countries in the world have signed the Convention; it is the most widely recognised human rights treaty.

Switzerland ratified the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1997, which means it adopted it as binding. Around 20 November there are events in many municipalities, often organised by **UNICEF Switzerland** and children's parliaments. Some municipalities hold UNICEF's “Child-friendly Municipality” award. There, children and young people are meant to have a say in projects such as playgrounds or routes to school.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rights that all children in the world have, for example to protection, education and having a say.

begriffe.wort: Convention on the Rights of the Child
begriffe.erklaerung: A UN agreement of 1989 that sets out children's rights.
The United Nations children's agency.
To adopt a treaty officially and as binding.

gewusst: The Convention on the Rights of the Child has been ratified by almost every state in the world; only the USA is missing.
On 20 November, in some cities an important building is lit up in blue, the colour of UNICEF.
In Japan there is a Children's Day on 5 May, when flags in the shape of carp are hung up.

teile.einleitung: UNESCO is the United Nations organisation for education, science and culture. It is best known for its World Heritage List, which includes famous buildings and natural wonders. There are many such World Heritage Sites in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: UNESCO works for education, science and culture.
It was founded in November 1945 and is based in Paris.
The abbreviation stands for “United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization”.
The World Heritage Convention to protect special places has existed since 1972.
Over 1200 sites worldwide are on the World Heritage List (as of 2025).
Switzerland has 13 World Heritage Sites, including the Old City of Bern and the Jungfrau-Aletsch area.
UNESCO also protects living traditions such as the Basel Carnival.

abschnitte.text: **UNESCO** is a specialised agency of the United Nations based in Paris. It was founded on 16 November 1945, shortly after the Second World War. The idea was: if people know more about each other and learn together, fewer wars will happen. Today almost all the states of the world are members, Switzerland since 1949.

One main aim is for every child to be able to go to school and learn to read and write. Many millions of children worldwide still do not go to school, especially girls in poor countries. UNESCO helps countries to build schools and train teachers. For example, it organises **International Literacy Day** on 8 September.

With the **World Heritage Convention** of 1972, states commit themselves to protecting especially valuable places. These include buildings such as the Pyramids of Giza or the Great Wall of China and natural wonders such as the Grand Canyon. If a World Heritage Site is threatened, it is put on the “red list” of World Heritage in Danger. Every year a committee decides which new places are added.

Switzerland's sites include the **Old City of Bern**, the Abbey of St Gall and the Benedictine Convent of St John at Müstair. The three castles of Bellinzona, the Lavaux vineyard terraces and the Rhaetian Railway on the Albula and Bernina lines are also World Heritage. Natural heritage sites are the Jungfrau-Aletsch region, Monte San Giorgio and the Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona. They also include, among others, the watchmaking towns of La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle.

Since 2003 UNESCO has also protected **intangible cultural heritage**, meaning traditions, festivals and crafts. From Switzerland these include the Basel Carnival, avalanche risk management and the craft of watchmaking, which was listed together with France. Such traditions only live on if people keep them up and pass them on. UNESCO also promotes science, for example ocean research.

begriffe.erklaerung: Places that are so valuable that they are protected for all of humanity.
An independent organisation that is closely linked to the UN.
Culture you cannot touch, such as customs, music or craft knowledge.
People learning to read and write.

gewusst: The Rhaetian Railway on the Albula and Bernina lines is one of the few railway lines in the world that are World Heritage.
At Monte San Giorgio in Ticino many fossils of marine reptiles from the Triassic period have been found.

teile.einleitung: Customs duty is a charge you have to pay when you bring goods across a national border. Customs also checks that no forbidden items come into the country. In Switzerland the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security is responsible for this.
wichtigste: Since 2022 the Swiss customs authority has been called the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security, FOCBS for short.
Anyone who secretly brings goods across the border is smuggling.
Since 2025 the duty-free allowance has been 150 francs per person per day.
With the QuickZoll app you can declare your purchases yourself.
Samnaun in the Grisons is an area outside the customs territory.
Souvenirs made of ivory may not be brought into Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: A **customs duty** is a fee on goods that are brought across a border. In the past customs duties were one of the Confederation's most important sources of income. Customs duties can also protect home-grown products, because imported goods become more expensive. But customs has other tasks too: it checks that no **forbidden goods** such as drugs or weapons come into the country. In Switzerland the **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security** (FOCBS) has been responsible since 2022.

Many people from Switzerland shop in nearby countries because many things are cheaper there. This is called **shopping tourism**. You may bring purchases back without paying VAT up to a certain value. Since **1 January 2025** this **duty-free allowance** has been **150 francs** per person per day; before that it was 300 francs. Additional quantity limits apply to meat, alcohol and tobacco. With the **QuickZoll** app you can declare and pay for goods before you reach the border.

Some things may not be brought in at all. These include souvenirs made of **ivory**. Ivory comes from the tusks of **elephants**. To protect these animals, trade in it is banned. Many products from other protected animals and plants are also not allowed. Anyone who brings such things back risks a penalty.

Anyone who brings goods across the border secretly and without declaring them is **smuggling**. This is forbidden and is punished. In the past people in the mountains smuggled things such as coffee, sugar or tobacco between Switzerland and Italy. The **Swiss Customs Museum** in **Cantine di Gandria** on **Lake Lugano** tells the story. It stands where there used to be a border post.

The village of **Samnaun** in the Grisons is an **area outside the customs territory**. It is part of Switzerland, but not part of the Swiss customs territory. You can buy many goods there without customs duty, for example perfume or petrol. The reason lies in history: for a long time Samnaun had only poor connections with the rest of Switzerland. Anyone driving from Samnaun back into the rest of Switzerland is checked at customs.

gewusst: Since 1 January 2024 Switzerland has no longer charged customs duties on industrial products, but it still does on agricultural products.
Before there was a federal tax on income, the Confederation was funded to a large extent by customs duties.

teile.einleitung: The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 ended the Thirty Years' War in Europe. It was negotiated in Münster and Osnabrück. It is especially important for Switzerland, because the Swiss Confederacy was then released from the Holy Roman Empire.
wichtigste: The Peace of Westphalia was concluded in Münster and Osnabrück in 1648.
It ended the Thirty Years' War and the Eighty Years' War.
The Basel mayor Johann Rudolf Wettstein achieved the Confederacy's release from the Empire.
Spain recognised the independence of the Netherlands.
As well as Catholics and Lutherans, the Reformed were also recognised.
France and Sweden received new territory.
The peace is often linked with the sovereignty of states.

abschnitte.text: The **Thirty Years' War** lasted in Europe from **1618 to 1648**. It was about religion, but also about power between rulers. Catholic and Protestant princes and foreign powers such as Sweden and France fought each other. Large parts of Germany were laid waste. In the end all sides were exhausted and ready to make peace.

The peace negotiations took place in two cities: the Catholic powers negotiated in **Münster**, the Protestant ones in **Osnabrück**. Both cities are in **Westphalia**, hence the name. The negotiations lasted several years. In January 1648 Spain and the Netherlands concluded the Peace of Münster. Spain recognised the **Republic of the United Netherlands**, and the **Eighty Years' War** came to an end.

The Basel mayor **Johann Rudolf Wettstein** travelled to Westphalia as the Confederacy's envoy. He achieved the release of the **Swiss Confederacy** from the jurisdiction of the **Holy Roman Empire**. This is regarded as its **independence under international law**. In fact the Confederacy had long been independent, but now this was officially recognised.

The **Peace of Augsburg** of 1555 had only recognised Catholics and Lutherans. In 1648 the **Reformed**, that is the Calvinists, were also included. For the ownership of church property a reference year was fixed, the **normative year 1624**. Ownership as it stood on 1 January 1624 was to be decisive. This was meant to end the dispute over churches and monasteries.

**France** received the Habsburg rights in **Alsace**. Its possession of the bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun was also confirmed. **Sweden** received, among other things, **Western Pomerania** on the Baltic as well as Bremen and Verden. The peace is often linked with the **sovereignty** of states: equal states that do not interfere in each other's internal affairs. Historians stress, however, that this picture partly only came about later.

gewusst: The Peace of Westphalia is regarded as one of the first great peace congresses, attended by almost all the powers of Europe.
In Basel today the Wettstein Bridge remembers Johann Rudolf Wettstein.

teile.einleitung: Before a vote you see colourful posters everywhere. They campaign for a yes or a no. In Switzerland these **referendum posters** are part of the **voting campaign**.
wichtigste: Referendum posters usually go up in the weeks before the vote.
You see them along roads and in squares.
They campaign for yes or no.
Parties and committees often make the posters and also pay for them.
You do not have to believe what a poster says; you should think for yourself.

abschnitte.text: A **referendum poster** is a large advertising picture. It is meant to persuade people to vote **yes** or **no** in a vote. Usually the yes or the no is written on it in big, easy-to-read letters. There is also a short sentence and an eye-catching picture. This way you understand the message even as you walk past.

Referendum posters usually go up in the **weeks before the vote**. You see them along **roads**, in squares, at stations and on fences. This period, in which people campaign with posters, advertisements and events, is called the **voting campaign**. After the vote the posters are taken down again.

**Parties** and **committees** often make the posters. A committee is a group of people who campaign for or against a proposal. Associations sometimes take part too. The **groups that campaign** pay for the posters themselves. Because people have different opinions, you often see posters for yes and for no side by side.

A poster only shows one side. It wants to persuade and sometimes exaggerates. That is why you do not have to believe what a poster says. You should **think for yourself** and also find information elsewhere, for example in the voting booklet or in the newspaper. This way you can form your own opinion.

gewusst: Some Swiss referendum posters are so famous that they are shown in museums today.
As well as posters, campaigns for votes are now also run on the internet and on social media.

teile.einleitung: The Sustainable Development Goals are 17 goals agreed by the countries of the UN. They include no poverty, education for all and climate action, to be achieved by 2030. They are meant to make the world fairer, more peaceful and kinder to the environment.
wichtigste: There are 17 Sustainable Development Goals.
They are known as the SDGs for short.
The UN adopted them in September 2015.
They are to be achieved by the year 2030, which is why people speak of the 2030 Agenda.
Examples are no poverty, zero hunger, education for all and climate action.
The goals apply to all countries, including rich countries such as Switzerland.
Many goals will probably not be fully achieved by 2030.

abschnitte.text: The **Sustainable Development Goals** are a shared plan of all UN member states. They consist of 17 main goals and 169 targets. Each goal has its own colour and its own symbol. Together they form the **2030 Agenda**.

As early as 2000 the UN had adopted eight **Millennium Development Goals**, which were meant mainly to help poorer countries. When these ran out in 2015, the countries worked out new goals. In September 2015 all 193 member states adopted the 2030 Agenda in New York. What was new was that the goals now apply to **all countries**.

Goal 1 is **no poverty** and Goal 2 zero hunger. Goal 4 calls for quality education for all children and young people. Goal 6 calls for clean water, Goal 5 for equality between women and men. Goal 13 is **climate action**, and Goals 14 and 15 protect life below water and on land.

**Sustainable** means living in such a way that later generations can still live well too. People think of three areas: the environment, society and the economy. One example is a forest where only as much wood is cut as grows back. The goals show that these areas are closely linked.

Switzerland has also committed itself to putting the goals into practice. For this the **Federal Council** has adopted a sustainable development strategy and reports regularly to the UN on progress. In Switzerland this is about, for example, emitting fewer greenhouse gases and throwing away less food. Municipalities, schools and companies also take part with their own projects.

begriffe.erklaerung: Acting in such a way that future generations can also live well.
The UN plan with the 17 goals that are to be achieved by 2030.
The abbreviation for Sustainable Development Goals.
All the people who were born at about the same time.

gewusst: The last of the 17 goals is partnerships for the goals, because no country can manage it alone.
You can see the colourful symbols of the 17 goals on posters, badges and even in school books.
Everyone can help, for example by producing less rubbish or using water sparingly.

tvudwrl.t: United Nations Economic and Social Council

teile.einleitung: The United Nations Economic and Social Council, ECOSOC for short, is one of the main bodies of the UN. It deals with the economy, social questions and the environment. It also coordinates the work of many UN organisations.
wichtigste: ECOSOC stands for Economic and Social Council.
The Council has 54 member states; when it was founded in 1945 there were 18.
The members are elected for three years.
ECOSOC can give non-governmental organisations consultative status.
It works closely with specialised agencies such as the WHO.
The Economic Commission for Europe is based in Geneva.

abschnitte.titel: A main body of the UN
abschnitte.text: The **Economic and Social Council** is one of the main bodies of the UN. Its abbreviation is **ECOSOC**. It deals with the **economy**, **social questions** and the **environment**. These include, for example, poverty, health, education and sustainable development. It makes recommendations and brings states, experts and organisations together.

When the UN was founded in 1945, ECOSOC had **18 members**. Through changes to the UN Charter it was enlarged to 27 in **1965** and to **54 members** in **1973**. Every year the **General Assembly** elects 18 states for a term of **three years**. So a third of the Council is renewed every year.

ECOSOC works closely with the **specialised agencies**, such as the **WHO** or the International Labour Organization. It coordinates their work. Under **Article 71** of the Charter it can give **non-governmental organisations** (NGOs) consultative status. In this way thousands of organisations may take part in UN meetings. ECOSOC also includes **five regional commissions**. The **Economic Commission for Europe** works in the Palais des Nations in **Geneva**.

ECOSOC has several **functional commissions**. Since **1946** the **Commission on the Status of Women** has worked for equality for women. It meets in New York every year. The **Commission on Human Rights** used to be one of them too. In **2006** it was replaced by the **Human Rights Council** in Geneva, which reports directly to the General Assembly.

Under the auspices of ECOSOC, the **High-level Political Forum**, HLPF for short, meets every July. There it is reviewed how the world is progressing on the **Sustainable Development Goals** of the **2030 Agenda**. States present voluntary national reviews. **Switzerland** has also reported there on how it is putting the goals into practice.

gewusst: Since it was founded, ECOSOC has grown to three times its size: from 18 to 54 members.
Several thousand non-governmental organisations have consultative status with ECOSOC.

teile.einleitung: On 3 March 2024 Switzerland voted on a **13th AHV pension**. The initiative was approved. This means pensioners receive an extra monthly pension once a year.
wichtigste: The initiative for a 13th AHV pension was approved on 3 March 2024 with 58.2 per cent voting yes.
Its official title was “For a better life in old age”.
For the first time, the people approved a left-wing initiative to expand the welfare state.
On the same day the pensions initiative was rejected with 74.7 per cent voting no.
The 13th pension will be paid from 2026.
This increases the annual AHV pension by around 8.3 per cent.

abschnitte.text: The popular initiative “For a better life in old age” was launched by the **Swiss Federation of Trade Unions**. It called for all AHV pensioners to receive a **13th monthly pension** every year. On 3 March 2024, 58.2 per cent of voters said yes. A majority of the cantons also agreed. The Federal Council and parliament had recommended rejecting the initiative.

The result is regarded as historic: for the first time the people approved a **left-wing initiative** to expand the welfare state. An important figure in the campaign was **Pierre-Yves Maillard**, the president of the Federation of Trade Unions. Supporters pointed to rising prices and rents. Opponents warned of the high costs for the AHV and asked how these would be paid for.

On the same day the **pensions initiative** of the Young Liberals was also put to the people. It wanted to raise the retirement age first to 66 and then link it to life expectancy. This initiative was clearly rejected, with 74.7 per cent voting no. So at the same time the people said yes to more pension and no to a higher retirement age.

The 13th pension will be paid from **2026**, once a year. An example: someone who receives an AHV monthly pension of 2000 francs used to get 12 times 2000, that is 24,000 francs a year. With the 13th pension it is 26,000 francs. That is an increase of one twelfth, or around **8.3 per cent**. After the vote, the Federal Council and parliament had to decide how the extra costs would be funded.

gewusst: Many employees in Switzerland are familiar with a 13th month's salary, which is where the idea of a 13th pension came from.
The AHV (old-age and survivors' insurance) is the first pillar of the Swiss pension system and has existed since 1948.

teile.einleitung: In 1994 a genocide took place in the East African country of Rwanda. In around 100 days mainly members of the Tutsi were killed, but also moderate Hutu. The genocide is one of the worst crimes of the 20th century.
wichtigste: The genocide in Rwanda began in April 1994 and lasted until July 1994.
Extremist Hutu directed it mainly against the Tutsi.
Estimates range from 800,000 to one million dead.
It was triggered by the shooting down of President Juvénal Habyarimana's plane on 6 April 1994.
The radio station RTLM stirred up violence.
The Rwandan Patriotic Front under Paul Kagame ended the genocide in July 1994.
A UN criminal tribunal in Arusha judged the main people responsible.

abschnitte.text: Rwanda is a small country in East Africa. Because it is very hilly and mostly lies over 1000 metres high, it is called the **land of a thousand hills**. The capital is **Kigali** in the centre of the country. Rwanda is home mainly to people who call themselves **Hutu** or **Tutsi**. They speak the same language, but in colonial times the groups were strictly separated and recorded on identity cards.

There had long been tension and violence between Hutu and Tutsi. On **6 April 1994** the plane of President **Juvénal Habyarimana** was shot down as it approached Kigali to land. That same night extremist Hutu began planned killings. They were directed mainly against Tutsi, but also against Hutu who wanted peace. By July an estimated 800,000 to one million people had been killed.

The radio station **RTLM** played a big part. It spread hatred against the Tutsi and openly called for violence. It insultingly called them “cockroaches”. Because many people had no television at that time, the radio reached a great many people. This shows how dangerous **propaganda** can be when people are presented as worth less than others.

The UN had only a few Blue Helmet soldiers in the country and could not prevent the killings. The rebel group **Rwandan Patriotic Front** conquered the country by July 1994 and stopped the genocide. Its leader **Paul Kagame** later became president. Many people then fled to neighbouring countries. Rwanda had to rebuild life together with great effort.

The UN set up an **International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda**. It sat in **Arusha** in Tanzania and judged the main people responsible. In Rwanda itself there were also traditional village courts called **Gacaca**. There, perpetrators and survivors came together. In Kigali a large **memorial** remembers the victims.

gewusst: The genocide in Rwanda lasted only around 100 days.
Before 1994 Switzerland was heavily involved in development cooperation in Rwanda.

teile.einleitung: **Aristotle** was a Greek philosopher who lived around 2300 years ago. He thought about how people can best live together and which form of state is good. His ideas still shape political thinking today.
wichtigste: Aristotle lived from 384 to 322 BC and was a pupil of Plato.
He was the teacher of the young Alexander the Great.
In his work “Politics” he examines the forms of state.
He distinguishes six forms of state: three good ones and three corrupt ones.
He always asks: who rules, and does the rule serve the common good?
For Aristotle the human being is a “zoon politikon”, a social being.

abschnitte.titel: The life of a great thinker
abschnitte.text: Aristotle was born in Stagira in northern Greece in 384 BC. As a young man he went to Athens and studied for about twenty years at Plato's **Academy**. Later King Philip II of Macedon brought him to his court. There Aristotle taught the king's son, who later became **Alexander the Great**. Back in Athens he founded his own school, the **Lyceum**.

Aristotle sorts the forms of state according to two criteria. First: does **one, a few or many** rule? Second: do they rule for the **common good** or for their own benefit? These questions give six forms of state. He even had many constitutions of Greek city-states collected and compared for this. His thoughts are set out in the work “Politics”.

If one person rules for the good of all, it is called **monarchy**; if he rules for his own benefit, it is **tyranny**. If a few rule well, it is **aristocracy**, the rule of the best. The corrupt form is **oligarchy**, the rule of the rich. Aristotle calls the good rule of the many **polity**. He calls the corrupt form of the many democracy, the rule of the poor for their own benefit.

abschnitte.titel: The human being as a social being
abschnitte.text: Aristotle describes the human being as a **zoon politikon**. This means that humans are by nature made for community. Only in the **polis**, the city-state, can they lead a good life. A person entirely alone, he said, could not fully develop. That is why, for Aristotle, politics is closely linked to the question of how to live well.

Today we understand something different by **democracy** than Aristotle did. For us it is a good form of state in which everyone has a say. But his question of whether a government serves the common good is still important today. The idea of a **mixed constitution**, combining elements of different forms, also lives on. Aristotle also wrote about ethics, nature, logic and much more.

gewusst: The later historian Polybius called the corrupt rule of the many “ochlocracy”, rule by the mob.
Aristotle is regarded as one of the most influential philosophers of all; his writings were studied throughout Europe in the Middle Ages.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who loses their job is not simply left without money. In Switzerland **unemployment insurance**, ALV for short, helps. It pays money and gives support in finding a new job.
wichtigste: Unemployment insurance has been compulsory for all employees since 1977.
The contribution is 2.2 per cent of salary; employees and employers each pay half.
Unemployed people usually receive 70 per cent of their insured salary as a daily allowance.
Anyone who has to support children receives 80 per cent.
You need at least 12 months of contributions in the last two years.
The Regional Employment Centres (RAV) give advice and help find jobs.
Short-time work compensation and insolvency compensation protect employees in crises.

abschnitte.text: The ALV is a **social insurance**, like the AHV or the disability insurance (IV). In the past the cantons could decide for themselves whether they wanted insurance against unemployment. Since 1977 **compulsory insurance** has applied to the whole of Switzerland. Today the **Unemployment Insurance Act** sets out the details. Anyone who is employed is automatically insured.

The ALV is funded mainly through **salary contributions**. In total these are 2.2 per cent of salary, up to an annual salary of 148,200 francs. Half of this, 1.1 per cent, is deducted directly from employees' pay. The **employer** pays the other half. On a payslip you can see the ALV deduction next to the AHV deduction.

Unemployed people receive a **daily allowance**. It is normally 70 per cent of their previous insured salary. Anyone who has to support children, had a low salary or has a disability receives 80 per cent. The condition is a **contribution period** of at least 12 months within two years. You must also make an active effort to find a new job.

abschnitte.titel: The RAV helps with job hunting
abschnitte.text: Anyone who becomes unemployed registers with the **Regional Employment Centre**, RAV for short. There they get advice and help with applications. The RAV passes on job vacancies and can suggest courses. It also checks whether you are writing enough applications. Anyone who does not make an effort can receive a lower daily allowance.

The ALV does not only pay daily allowances. With **short-time work**, employees temporarily work less, and the ALV covers part of the lost pay. This means companies do not have to dismiss their staff. During the coronavirus pandemic this helped a great many businesses. If an employer goes bankrupt, **insolvency compensation** pays the outstanding wages for a limited time.

gewusst: During the coronavirus pandemic, at times over a million people in Switzerland were on short-time work.
There is also bad-weather compensation, for example for building workers when they cannot work because of the weather.

teile.einleitung: Sovereignty means that a state decides its own affairs. Internally it holds the highest power, and externally it is independent of other states. The concept is very important for how states live together.
wichtigste: A sovereign state decides its own affairs.
Jean Bodin coined the term in the 16th century.
With the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, the independence of the Swiss Confederation was recognised.
The cantons are sovereign insofar as the Federal Constitution does not limit this.
In the UN General Assembly each state has one vote.
Popular sovereignty means that all state power comes from the people.

abschnitte.text: A **sovereign** state holds the highest power **internally**. It makes the laws and enforces them. **Externally** it is **independent** of other states. No other state may give it orders. This includes **territorial sovereignty**: the laws of this state apply on its own territory. **Personal sovereignty**, on the other hand, concerns the state's own citizens, even abroad.

The French thinker **Jean Bodin** coined the term in the **16th century**. In 1576, in his “Six Books of the Commonwealth”, he described sovereignty as the **highest and perpetual power** in the state. At that time wars of religion were raging in France. Bodin was looking for a strong order that would secure peace.

The **Peace of Westphalia** of **1648** ended the Thirty Years' War. With it, the independence of the **Swiss Confederation** from the **Holy Roman Empire** was also recognised. The peace is regarded as the beginning of an order of **sovereign states with equal rights** in Europe. From this follows the **principle of non-interference**: states may not interfere in the internal affairs of other states. Today it is laid down in the UN Charter.

The UN is based on the principle of the **sovereign equality** of all member states. That is why each state has **one vote** in the **General Assembly**. Small Switzerland has just as much voting power there as a large country. In the Security Council, however, there are differences, because five states have a veto there.

According to **Article 3** of the Federal Constitution, the **cantons** are sovereign insofar as their sovereignty is not limited by the **Federal Constitution**. Everything that has not been assigned to the Confederation is regulated by the cantons themselves. **Popular sovereignty** is also important: all state power comes from the **people**. In Switzerland this shows especially in **popular votes** and **initiatives**.

gewusst: The Federal Constitution expressly calls the cantons “sovereign”.
Since the Peace of Westphalia of 1648, the Swiss Confederation has also been legally independent of the Holy Roman Empire.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland three levels take care of the tasks of the state: **the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities**. The Confederation takes on tasks that must be regulated in the same way for the whole country. Much of the rest stays with the cantons and municipalities.
wichtigste: The Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities share the tasks; this is called federalism.
The Confederation is responsible for the army and national defence.
Foreign policy and treaties with other states are a matter for the Confederation.
The Confederation sets the traffic rules and road signs.
The police are mainly a matter for the cantons.
MeteoSwiss, a federal office, warns of severe weather.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland is a **federal state**. It is made up of the Confederation, 26 cantons and many municipalities. This division is called **federalism**. The Federal Constitution sets out which tasks the Confederation has. Anything that is not given to the Confederation there stays with the **cantons**. They pass some tasks on to the **municipalities**.

**National defence** is a task of the Confederation. That is why there is a single Swiss Army. **Foreign policy** also belongs to the Confederation. It looks after relations with other countries and concludes treaties with them. The Confederation also controls the borders and collects **customs duties**.

Some things must be the same throughout the country. The Confederation makes the **traffic rules** and decides what road signs look like. That is why a stop sign in Geneva looks the same as one in St Gallen. Money is also a matter for the Confederation: the **Swiss franc** is valid everywhere. The Confederation is also responsible for the **national roads** and important social insurances such as the AHV.

For its tasks the Confederation has many **federal offices**. One example is **MeteoSwiss**, the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology. It makes weather forecasts and issues official **severe weather warnings**. Other offices deal with things such as health, roads or the environment. Together they form the **federal administration**.

The Confederation does not do everything. The **police** are mainly a matter for the cantons, which is why there is a cantonal police force in every canton. **Schools** and hospitals are also among the cantons' tasks. The municipalities look after things such as rubbish, water and school buildings. This way many decisions are made close to the people.

gewusst: The Confederation may only take on tasks that the Federal Constitution gives it. New federal tasks require a vote of the people and the cantons.
The federal administration has its headquarters in Bern, but many federal offices are in other towns; MeteoSwiss, for example, is in Zurich.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who is elected to an office does not stay there for ever. After a certain time there is a new election. This time is called a **term of office**.
wichtigste: A term of office is the time during which someone holds an office.
The four-year term of the parliament in Bern is called a legislative period.
Newly elected members of the National Council start work in December.
In the Council of States a term of office lasts four years in most cantons.
The President of the USA is in office for four years, the President of France for five years.
At the end of a term of office there is a new election.

abschnitte.titel: What a term of office is
abschnitte.text: A **term of office** is the time during which someone holds an office, for example as mayor of a municipality or member of the National Council. At the end of the term there is a **new election**. Anyone who wants to can often stand again. Terms of office do not last for ever, so that the **people can decide again** who should represent them. This keeps power under control.

The National Council is elected every four years in October. The newly elected members start work in **December**, in the winter session. The parliament's four-year term is called the **legislative period**. In the **Council of States**, too, a term of office lasts **four years** in most cantons. At the start of the legislative period, parliament also elects the Federal Council again.

In other countries terms of office vary in length. The **President of the USA** is elected for **four years** and may be elected no more than twice. The **President of France** is in office for **five years**. In France it used to be as long as seven years. In many countries it is set out exactly how often someone may be re-elected.

In Switzerland there are also very short terms of office. The **President of the Confederation** is only in office for one year; after that another member of the Federal Council takes over. The presidencies of the National Council and the Council of States also change every year. In many municipalities a term of office lasts four years.

gewusst: There is no limit on how often members of the Federal Council may be re-elected.
In France the president's term of office was shortened from seven to five years by a referendum in 2000.

teile.einleitung: Many people live in Switzerland who do not have a Swiss passport. They work, go to school and are part of everyday life. Their rights depend on their permit and on where they live.
wichtigste: In 2023 around a quarter of the permanent resident population did not have a Swiss passport.
The largest foreign group comes from Italy.
Anyone who comes to work often receives permit B, and later permit C.
Only Swiss citizens may take part in national votes.
In Neuchâtel and Jura foreigners may also vote at cantonal level.
Cross-border commuters live abroad and work in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Most foreigners in Switzerland come from **Europe**. The largest group comes from **Italy**, with over 300,000 people. They are followed by Germany and Portugal. Many Italians came as workers as early as the 1950s and 1960s. Someone who moves to a new country is an **immigrant**; someone who leaves their country is an emigrant.

Anyone who comes to Switzerland to work often receives **permit B**, the residence permit. Anyone who has lived here for a long time can get **permit C**, the settlement permit. This is usually possible after 5 or 10 years. **Cross-border commuters** have their own permit, permit G. They live, for example, in France, Italy or Germany and travel to work in Switzerland regularly.

Only Swiss citizens may take part in **national** elections and votes. In some cantons it is different. In **Neuchâtel** and **Jura**, foreigners who have lived there for a long time may also take part in cantonal votes. In the canton of **Vaud** they may vote and stand in elections in the municipality, but not in the canton. Most German-speaking cantons have no voting rights for foreigners.

Some people do not come voluntarily. **Refugees** have to leave their homes because they are in danger there because of war or persecution. Switzerland takes in refugees and protects them. Whether someone is recognised as a refugee is examined by the **State Secretariat for Migration**. Switzerland has signed international agreements on this.

Anyone who has lived in Switzerland for a long time can apply for **naturalisation**. Among other things, this requires permit C and, as a rule, ten years of residence. You must be well **integrated** and speak a national language. The Confederation, the canton and the municipality all have a say in naturalisation. After that you may vote and stand in elections everywhere.

gewusst: Many people without a Swiss passport were born and grew up in Switzerland.
In the canton of Geneva the proportion of foreigners is much higher than the Swiss average.
